topic.name: Early Maths Vocabulary
topic.description: Use mathematical words carefully when counting, comparing, and describing shapes and positions
evidence: Use 'more than', 'fewer than', and 'the same as' correctly when comparing groups
Name shapes correctly and describe their features using words like 'sides' and 'corners'
Use positional words (above, below, next to) precisely to describe where objects are
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} talks about maths — like comparing numbers or describing shapes — do they use the right words, like "larger than", "fewer", "beside", or "corner"?

pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, attending to precision means using mathematical words carefully — 'more than / fewer than / the same as' for comparing, shape names with 'sides' and 'corners', and positional words (above, below, next to) — and beginning to refine vague everyday language into words that pin down the meaning. The EEF Early Years guidance frames this as a staged informal→formal journey: start from a child's own words ('pointy', 'big') and help them rephrase precisely ('has points', 'taller'). A key move is exposing children to a WIDE VARIETY of examples of each shape so they do not form a narrow, prototype-bound concept (only a 'point-up' triangle counts).
bestPractices: Seize everyday moments to reinforce precise vocabulary — who is 'first', who has 'more than', where the teddy is 'behind' — rather than teaching words in isolation (EEF)
Help children refine ambiguous everyday words: when a child says 'big', ask 'taller, or more?' so they choose the word that carries the meaning (EEF's big→tall example)
Move informal→formal: accept 'pointy'/'curved' first, then introduce formal shape names gradually and reinforce them in routine (EEF)
Expose children to varied examples and non-examples of each shape (many kinds of triangle, tilted squares) to prevent an over-generalised, prototype-only concept (EEF)
Pair each word with the action or feature it names — run a finger along a SIDE, point to a CORNER — so the vocabulary is grounded, not recited
keyRepresentations: Comparison language with matched groups (more than / fewer than / same as)
A varied shape gallery (many triangles, rotated squares) with sides and corners traced
Positional-language scenes (objects above/below/behind/next to)
Real objects and manipulatives named in play
commonMisconceptions: Uses ambiguous everyday words where a precise one exists — 'big' for tall or for 'more', 'by' for a specific position (EEF)
Recognises only prototype shapes — rejects a long or upside-down triangle as 'not a triangle', calls a tilted square a 'diamond' (EEF: needs varied exposure)
Uses 'sides' and 'corners' interchangeably, or counts corners when asked for sides
Thinks a shape's name depends on how it is turned or how big it is, rather than its properties

learn.summary: For children aged 5-6, attending to precision means using mathematical words carefully: comparison words ('more than / fewer than / the same as'), shape vocabulary ('sides', 'corners', shape names), and positional words (above, below, behind, next to). A key proposed teaching move is to make vague language have a visible consequence so the child can discover the value of a precise word — a research-informed approach rather than a uniquely required method — following an informal→formal journey that starts from the child's own words ('pointy', 'big') and helps them rephrase ('has points', 'taller'). Children also need exposure to a WIDE VARIETY of examples of each shape so they do not form a narrow, prototype-bound concept.

activities.title: Tell the literal robot where teddy goes
feedback: When the child says 'by the box' and the robot puts teddy near the box but not where the child meant (e.g. behind it instead of on top), the mismatch itself is the feedback — prompt: 'Did the robot put teddy where you wanted? How could you say it so teddy lands exactly there?'
If the child says 'bigger' and is handed the taller-but-fewer tower, ask 'Do you mean taller, or more blocks?' and have the CHILD choose the precise word rather than supplying it.
When the child uses a precise word and the robot succeeds first time, name the success: 'On top of told the robot exactly where — it worked straight away.'
activities.rationale: Precision of communication becomes meaningful when vagueness has an immediate, repeatable consequence the child can see and repair. A responsive surface (or in-role character) lets the child produce and refine language rather than merely recognise it, following EEF's informal→formal refinement (big→tall). This is a proposed design, not a validated or uniquely-best format.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
Mathematically proficient students communicate precisely, use clear definitions, and in the elementary grades give carefully formulated explanations to each other
learnerActions: Direct a friendly robot (or puppet/character) to place teddy somewhere, e.g. say 'put teddy by the box'.

Watch the robot do EXACTLY what the words say — 'by the box' only means near the box, so the robot might put teddy behind it, in front of it, or beside it — so the ambiguity can produce a result that is not where the child meant.
Refine the instruction to a precise positional word ('on top of the box', 'behind the box') and check the robot now gets it right.
Repeat with a comparison round: ask for 'the tower with MORE blocks' rather than 'the bigger tower', to distinguish taller from more.
Say, in the child's own words, why the exact word helped the robot understand.
activities.intendedInsight: A vague everyday word (like 'by' or 'big') often fails to pin down the meaning; choosing a precise word (on top of / behind; taller / more) lets a listener do exactly what you intend.

activities.title: A character who takes your words literally
feedback: When the character deliberately misunderstands, prompt the child to explain which precise word they meant.
Praise the moment the child spontaneously refines: 'You changed by to behind so I knew exactly where.'
activities.rationale: An in-role character who misunderstands can generate precise-language repair through unscripted, responsive dialogue, giving the child spoken production practice. Short turns suit the age. This is a proposed format; the sources do not establish it as superior to other media.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
learnerActions: Talk with a playful character (puppet or robot friend) who cheerfully misunderstands vague instructions, e.g. 'You said BY the box, so I put teddy BEHIND it — right?'
Answer the character's clarifying questions to pin down the position, comparison, or shape word you meant.
Keep each exchange short, and restate the instruction precisely until the character gets it right.
activities.intendedInsight: Being asked 'did you mean this or that?' makes a child notice an ambiguity and reach for the word that removes it — the repair IS the practice.

activities.title: The varied shape gallery (sides, corners and non-prototypes)
feedback: If the child rejects a long or upside-down triangle, show more varied examples and non-examples and return focus to the defining property: a closed shape with three straight sides.
If the child calls a tilted square a 'diamond', count the four equal sides and four square (right-angle) corners together and confirm it is still a square however it is turned.
If the child swaps 'sides' and 'corners', re-pair each word with its action (run a finger along a side, point to a corner) in play rather than marking it wrong — it resolves with exposure.
activities.rationale: Varied examples and non-examples counter the prototype-only concept. A tap-to-reveal gallery can label and prime the vocabulary; on its own it primes recognition and does not require the child to produce or refine language, so pair it with the directing/dialogue activities.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
learnerActions: Explore a gallery of many triangles and quadrilaterals shown in varied orientations and sizes — long thin triangles, upside-down triangles, tilted squares.
Trace a finger along each SIDE and point to each CORNER as they are named, then reveal the shape's name.

Decide whether a tilted square is still a square (it has four equal sides and four square corners, however it is turned) and whether a long or upside-down triangle is still a triangle (it is a closed shape with three straight sides).
Sort a tilted square into the 'square' group by its properties rather than by how it looks or how it is turned.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's name depends on its properties (its straight sides and its corners), not on its size or orientation; 'side' and 'corner' name different features.

activities.title: Place the object in a spatial scene
feedback: If the placement does not match the word used, ask which word would describe where teddy actually is.
Confirm when the chosen word and the placement agree: 'Behind — and that's just where you put it.'
activities.rationale: Positional vocabulary is genuinely spatial, so placing an object in a scene (a simple room or picture) exercises that strand concretely. This supports only the positional strand; the comparison and shape-name strands are not spatial, so this activity is a companion rather than the main vehicle.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
learnerActions: Place teddy in a scene above, below, behind, or next to another object, choosing the positional word that matches where you want it.
Describe aloud where you put teddy using the precise positional word.
Swap roles: a partner states a position and you place teddy to match, then check it agrees.
activities.intendedInsight: Positional language describes genuine spatial relationships; the right word lets another person find the object exactly.

constraints: Seize everyday moments to reinforce precise vocabulary — who is 'first', who has 'more than', where the teddy is 'behind' — rather than teaching words in isolation.

Build informal→formal: accept the child's own words ('pointy', 'curved', 'big') first, then introduce and reinforce formal words gradually; have the CHILD choose the precise word rather than simply supplying it.
Pair each word with the action or feature it names (run a finger along a side, point to a corner) so vocabulary is grounded, not recited.
Treat interchangeable use of 'sides' and 'corners' as a developmental stage that resolves with exposure, not an error to drill or mark wrong.

A picture-word matching or tap-to-reveal task can check or prime recognition but does not by itself elicit the child producing or refining language; use it as a warm-up alongside the directing/dialogue activities, not as the sole vehicle.
The spatial-scene activity supports only the positional strand; it does not exercise comparison or shape-name vocabulary.

Diagnostic prompts deliberately use an ambiguous word (e.g. 'by') so the vagueness is detectable; a precise word like 'behind' would not reveal whether the child attends to precision. Responses are surfaced for discussion, not marked right or wrong.

When naming a square, use the properties that define it (four equal sides and four square corners), so a non-square rhombus is not accepted as a square; the teaching point is that turning a shape does not change its identity.

The legacy entry asserted that precision 'is best taught' by a live surface with a literal robot and framed alternatives as unable to make the child produce or refine language. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources; they have been softened to scoped proposals noting each format's affordance and limit, including in the summary.

Both cited sources (CCSS MP6 and EEF Early Maths) are general-practice guidance, not evaluations of the proposed robot game, puppet dialogue, or gallery; no comparative efficacy among these formats is established.

The original row defined a tilted square as a square by 'four equal sides' alone; this under-specifies a square (a rhombus also has four equal sides). Corrected in the learner action, feedback and constraints to include four square corners while keeping the age-appropriate focus on orientation invariance.

Is this one [a long thin triangle] a triangle? How do you know?

responseLevels.gap: Uses vague everyday words and does not notice the ambiguity; names only prototype shapes; conflates sides and corners.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, chooses precise comparison, shape and positional words, notices when a word is ambiguous and refines it, recognises varied (non-prototype) examples by their properties, and can say why saying it exactly helps the listener.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, offers a more precise word (taller, on top of) and names common shapes, but does not spontaneously refine vague language or accept non-prototype examples.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Showing Your Working
topic.description: Show and tell how a mathematical answer was found using objects, drawings, and spoken words
evidence: Use objects or drawings to demonstrate how an addition or subtraction was solved
Respond to 'how do you know?' by pointing to objects or a drawing and describing what was done
Listen to a peer's explanation and say whether they agree or disagree
topic.assessmentPrompt: After {{name}} solves a maths problem, can they explain how they got their answer — using counters, a drawing, or words — rather than just writing down the final number?

pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, 'showing your working' is the first rung of mathematical argument: the child shows and tells HOW an answer was found — with objects, a drawing, or spoken words — and begins to respond to 'how do you know?' by pointing to what they did rather than just restating the answer. On the NRICH novice-to-expert ladder this is the describing (and beginning-to-explain) stage. The crucial teaching insight is that at this age a child's REASONING typically runs ahead of their ability to COMMUNICATE it: a child who says little may nonetheless have reasoned soundly. So teaching separates the two — building the habit of demonstrating a method concretely, and, separately, scaffolding the language to narrate it — and treats listening to a peer and agreeing/disagreeing as the seed of critiquing reasoning.
bestPractices: Ask 'how do you know?' and 'show me' routinely, accepting objects, pointing, and drawings as valid ways to show working
Separate reasoning from its communication — judge whether a quiet child needs help thinking or help putting it into words, and support each differently
Model narrating a method aloud ('first I… then I…') and provide simple spoken stems
Use concrete referents (counters, ten frames, drawings) as the medium of explanation, as elementary arguments legitimately rest on objects and actions
Have children listen to a peer's method and say whether they agree, beginning to evaluate reasoning rather than just answers
Value the demonstration itself; do not treat limited vocabulary as limited mathematics
keyRepresentations: Concrete objects / counters moved to enact and show a method
Ten frame and part-part-whole drawing
Number sentence alongside the objects
Spoken sentence stems ('first… then… so…')
The describe → explain step of the NRICH reasoning ladder
commonMisconceptions: Restating the answer ('because it's 8') when asked 'how do you know?' instead of showing the method
A quiet or brief response mistaken for weak reasoning, when it is really communication that lags
Judging a peer's work only by whether the answer matches, not by whether the method makes sense
Believing 'showing your working' means writing the sum again rather than revealing the thinking

learn.summary: For 5-6 year olds, 'showing your working' means demonstrating and narrating HOW an answer was found — with objects, drawings, or spoken words — and beginning to answer 'how do you know?' by pointing to what was done rather than restating the answer. A key teaching insight is that at this age reasoning can often run ahead of the ability to communicate it: a quiet child may have reasoned soundly. Teaching therefore separates two threads — building the habit of demonstrating a method concretely, and separately scaffolding the language to narrate it — and treats listening to a peer and agreeing/disagreeing as the first seed of evaluating reasoning, not just answers.

activities.title: The curious listener who wants to know HOW
feedback: When the child shows and narrates a method, reflect it back as a short story so they hear their own doing turned into an explanation.
Accept spoken, pointed, tapped, or dragged responses, and never penalise sparse words — value the demonstration itself.
If the child only restates '8' or 'because it's right', prompt 'show me with your counters' and 'point to where the 3 went'.
When presenting a muddled-but-correct route, help the child attend to the steps rather than accept it just because the answer matched; make clear the muddled route is not the model to copy.
activities.rationale: Showing and telling how you worked something out is inherently dialogic. A character that keeps asking 'how do you know? show me!' and genuinely listens — accepting objects and pointing — rehearses the describe/explain habit and gives the child a reason to narrate a method aloud, which is where communication of reasoning is built. A deliberately wrong-but-plausible worked route plants the first seed of judging reasoning rather than answers. These are research-informed design proposals, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents (objects, drawings, diagrams, actions), and students at all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask questions to improve them.

Reasoning develops along a describe → explain → convince → justify → prove spectrum; the reasoning itself and the communication of it are distinct and often develop at different rates, with young children's reasoning frequently ahead of their ability to communicate it.
learnerActions: Solve a within-10 problem such as 5 and 3 using counters (physical objects or on-screen draggable counters).
When asked 'how did you get 8? show me!', move or point to the counters to re-enact the method — for example, 'I put 5, then counted on 3 more'.
Hear the method echoed back as a little story ('first you put 5, then you counted on 3 more, so you got 8') and notice that explaining = showing the doing, not repeating the answer.
Watch the listener solve a problem its own way — sometimes by a muddled or wrong route — and answer 'do you agree with how I did it? how can you tell?'
activities.intendedInsight: 'How do you know?' is answered by demonstrating the method, not by restating the answer; and a method can be judged by whether its steps make sense, not only by whether the final number is right.

activities.title: Show-how workspace with a compare-two-methods panel
feedback: Prompt the child to narrate alongside the replay so the demonstration and its words are built together.
On the compare panel, ask the child to point to the specific step they agree or disagree with rather than give a yes/no.
Treat a correct answer reached by an odd route as a chance to notice the method, not to approve it automatically.
activities.rationale: A workspace where the child moves counters or ten-frames to show a method and then narrates it makes the demonstration concrete and repeatable; a simple 'do you agree?' comparison introduces evaluating reasoning. Draggable counters, a replay of the steps, and a side-by-side compare panel are illustrative interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms, and are not validated here.
sourceClaims: Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents (objects, drawings, diagrams, actions), and students at all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask questions to improve them.
learnerActions: Move counters or fill a ten frame to solve an addition or subtraction, then use a 'show how you did it' replay to retrace the steps.
Narrate the recaptured steps aloud using stems such as 'first… then… so…'.
View a peer's or character's method beside your own and decide 'do you agree?', then 'show why' by pointing to a step that does or does not make sense.
activities.intendedInsight: A method can be made concrete, repeatable, and comparable; evaluating reasoning means looking at the steps, not only matching the final answer.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal a worked method (modelling scaffold)
feedback: Use the revealed stages as a model, then quickly move the child to demonstrating their own method so they do not only watch.
Name each revealed step in 'first… then… so…' form so the language of narration is modelled.
activities.rationale: Revealing a worked method's steps one at a time can model what showing your working looks like, but the child watches rather than demonstrates their own thinking, so it should lead into own-method demonstration. Recognition of a modelled method does not by itself elicit the child producing and narrating one. This is a modelling scaffold whose effectiveness is untested by the cited sources, not a substitute for the child producing and narrating a method.
learnerActions: Tap each stage of an already-solved problem to reveal 'what I did and why' at that step.
Afterwards, re-solve a fresh problem and show your own steps with objects or a drawing, narrating as you go.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the stages of a worked method named out loud shows what 'showing your working' can look like before producing one's own.

constraints: The target is demonstrating AND beginning to evaluate a method — not producing a single scored answer. An answer-only, scored format can record only the final result and cannot capture showing or telling a method, and it tends to reward the answer-restating this topic must move beyond; if used at all, treat it as a check of the final result, not of the reasoning.
A tap-to-reveal worked example is a modelling scaffold: the child watches rather than demonstrates, so it must be followed by the child producing and narrating their own method.

Separate reasoning from its communication: when a child is quiet or brief, judge whether they need help thinking or help putting it into words, and support that thread. Do not treat limited vocabulary as limited mathematics, and do not drill vocabulary in isolation.
Elementary arguments legitimately rest on objects, pointing, and drawings; accept these as valid ways to show working rather than requiring written sums or rich sentences.
At this age, full critique of a peer's reasoning is only emerging; expect the child to begin attending to steps (e.g. 'can you show what I did?') rather than deliver a complete evaluation.

Showing arithmetic working here does not need elaborate 3D spatial environments: simple concrete arrangements such as counters and ten frames are useful for showing a method, but complex spatial/3D manipulation is not needed for this objective, though it may serve other topics.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified in this independent review, and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit of every summary, insight, action, feedback, constraint and note found no new critical learner-facing errors or unsupported categorical claims; the previously flagged activities[2].sourceClaims=[] correction is confirmed already applied.

The included diagnostic routine (solve 5+3 with counters, ask 'how do you know? show me', then model an alternative or deliberately slipped method and ask 'do you agree?') is arithmetically sound: 5+3=8. No numeric errors were found in the source examples.

A deliberately 'wrong way' demonstration by the character should remain clearly a muddled route to test the child's attention to steps; ensure any wrong demonstration is not left as the child's takeaway model of correct method.

The tap-to-reveal activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because neither cited claim directly supports the efficacy of a watch-first modelling scaffold; the claims concern reasoning development generally, not evidence that this interaction helps.

The original source framed an answer-only scored format and a 3D/spatial format as 'poor fit'; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal 'cannot teach' claims.

'Can you tell me the first thing you did, and the next thing?' (scaffolds narrating the method)
'I'll do it my way — watch. Do you agree with how I did it?' (evaluating a method, not an answer)
Counterexample: solve it by a muddled route that still lands on 8 — does the child notice the method was odd, or accept it because the answer is right?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who responds to 'how do you know?' by SHOWING the method (moving or pointing to counters, or drawing) and telling it in some form ('I had 5, then 3 more'), and who, watching your method, judges it by whether the actions make sense rather than only whether the answer matches. Demonstrating the method and beginning to evaluate a method are the targets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reasoning runs ahead of communication — the child clearly used a sound method but 'just tells the answer' or cannot yet put the how into words.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT conclude the child cannot reason, and do not drill vocabulary in isolation. Ask them to SHOW with counters and narrate alongside; decide whether it is the reasoning or the communication that needs developing, and support that one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'how do you know?', the child gives the correct answer and a shrug or a single word, yet can correctly re-do the problem when watched — the thinking is there, the language is not.

errorPatterns.pattern: Restates the answer when asked 'how do you know?' ('because it's 8') instead of showing the method.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the move explicitly: 'show me with your counters', 'point to where the 3 went'; model narrating a method so the child hears what 'how' sounds like.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child repeats the result rather than demonstrating; the show-and-tell habit is not yet triggered by the prompt.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges a peer's (or teacher's) method only by whether the answer matches, not by whether the steps make sense.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not expect full critique yet; ask 'can you show what I did?' so the child attends to the steps, and use agree/disagree talk with clear listening turns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shown a method that reaches the right answer by a muddled route, the child agrees simply because the answer is right; evaluating the reasoning itself is only emerging.

responseLevels.gap: Gives only the answer or 'because it's right'; cannot show the method even with objects; judges others solely by the answer.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously demonstrates the method with objects/drawing and narrates it in some form, and when watching another method attends to whether the steps make sense — the seed of critiquing reasoning — not just the answer.
responseLevels.partial: Shows and describes WHAT they did with objects or a drawing (the describing step), but not yet WHY, and needs prompting; begins to look at a peer's steps only when asked.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child counters and a problem like 5 + 3. Once they have 8, ask: 'How do you know it's 8? Show me and tell me how you worked it out.' Then solve it yourself a different way (or with a deliberate slip), and ask: 'Do you agree with how I did it? How can you tell?' Treat it as a conversation about their thinking, not a marked answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child developing this practice turns 'how do you know?' into a demonstration — they re-enact the doing. A child at answer-only restates '8' or 'because it's right' and, when judging your method, checks only the final number. Because a young child's words may lag their thinking, the tell is whether they can SHOW the method (with objects) even when they cannot fully narrate it — not the richness of their vocabulary.

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7 precision extends from words to SYMBOLS and UNITS. Three strands: use the equals sign to mean 'is the same as' (both sides balance) rather than 'the answer comes next'; always include a unit with a measurement ('12 cm', not '12'); and use precise terms for 3-D shapes (edge, vertex, face) and comparisons (greater than, less than). The equals-sign strand is the load-bearing one: Falkner, Levi and Carpenter documented that most primary children read '=' operationally, so a running chain like 7+5=12+3=15 looks fine to them — teaching must confront this directly with true/false and open number sentences and a balance image.
bestPractices: Teach '=' as balance from the start — use true/false sentences (is 7+5=12+3 true?) and open sentences (8+4=□+5) so it means 'the same as', not 'write the answer' (Falkner/Levi/Carpenter)
Insist a measurement answer carries its unit — '12 what?' — because a bare number does not say how much (CCSS: specify units)
Name and touch the parts of 3-D shapes: face (a flat surface), edge (where two faces meet), vertex (a corner point), so words attach to features
State the meaning of the symbols used (=, >, <) and read them aloud in words, so notation carries agreed meaning (CCSS)
Value carefully formulated explanations — have children say the sentence in words and check both sides agree
keyRepresentations: Pan balance / balance scale for the equals sign
True/false and open number sentences
3-D shapes with face, edge, vertex labelled and handled
Measurement answers written with units (12 cm, 3 kg)
Comparison statements with >, <, =
commonMisconceptions: Reads '=' operationally as 'the answer is / and then', writing running chains like 7+5=12+3=15 (Falkner/Levi/Carpenter)
Fills 8+4=□+5 with 12 (the total so far) or 17 (everything added), not 7
Omits units, giving '12' for a length that is 12 cm — treating the unit as optional (CCSS)
Describes 3-D shapes with 2-D or loose words — 'corner' for vertex, 'side' for face, or calls a cube a 'square'

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, extend precision from words to symbols and units across three strands: (1) read '=' relationally as 'is the same as / both sides balance', not operationally as 'the answer comes next'; (2) always attach a unit to a measurement ('12 cm', not '12'); (3) use precise vocabulary for 3-D shapes (face, edge, vertex) and comparisons (greater than, less than). The equals-sign strand is the load-bearing one: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter documented that most primary children read '=' operationally, so a running chain like 7+5=12+3=15 looks correct to them. Confront this directly with true/false sentences, open number sentences, and a balance representation. A pan-balance interaction can make the meaning concrete, but a dialogue partner, a rotatable 3-D model, and screener items each serve distinct purposes and are preserved below.

activities.title: Weigh the sentence: does '=' balance?
feedback: If the child says 7+5=12+3 is fine because they 'did the steps', show the pans: 12 does not weigh the same as 15, so the sentence cannot be true even though each step was computed correctly.
If 8+4=□+5 is filled with 12 (the running total) or 17 (everything added), point back to the pans — the left side already weighs 12, so the right side needs 7 to level, not 12 or 17.
When the child rebalances a false sentence into a true one, confirm that both sides now weigh the same and have them read the whole sentence aloud in words.
activities.rationale: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter found most primary children read '=' operationally and that true/false and open number sentences build the relational 'is the same as' meaning. A live balance representation lets a child see non-equal sides and construct balanced open sentences by direct manipulation. The optional tipping/levelling animation can make the relational meaning concrete; it is an example mechanism, not the only route.
sourceClaims: Most primary children interpret '=' operationally as 'the answer is', so few correctly complete 8+4=□+5 (they give 12 or 17); true/false and open number sentences build the relational 'is the same as' meaning
Proficient students state the meaning of the symbols they choose, using the equal sign consistently and appropriately, and are careful about specifying units of measure
learnerActions: Take a friend's working, 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 = 15, and look only at the middle part: 7 + 5 = 12 + 3.

Using identical cubes (each cube weighs the same), place 7+5 cubes on the left pan and 12+3 cubes on the right pan of a pan balance and observe which way it tips (left holds 12 cubes, right holds 15, so the heavier right pan sinks and the lighter left pan rises — it does not balance).
Say aloud what '=' promises: both sides weigh the same.
Decide whether 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 is true or false, and explain using the balance.
Make both sides the same a different way, e.g. check that 3 + 5 = 6 + 2 (both are 8).
Complete an open sentence like 8 + 4 = □ + 5 by making the pans level, and say what number balances it (7).
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign means the two sides are the same amount; it is not an arrow pointing to the next answer. A running chain like 7+5=12+3=15 misuses '='. A balance that tips or levels makes this relationship visible.

activities.title: '12 what?' — the unit is part of the answer
feedback: If the child gives a bare '12' and is untroubled by '12 what?', contrast 12 cm with 12 m so the difference in size is obvious.
Confirm when the child spontaneously includes a unit and can explain why '12' alone is ambiguous.
activities.rationale: CCSS MP6 states proficient students are careful about specifying units of measure. An optional 'measuring station that refuses a bare number until a unit is chosen' can make this requirement concrete, but the core aim is that the child states and justifies the unit, not that any particular gating mechanism is used.
sourceClaims: Proficient students state the meaning of the symbols they choose, using the equal sign consistently and appropriately, and are careful about specifying units of measure
learnerActions: Measure an object (e.g. a pencil) and give the measurement.
When you answer '12', state the unit: 12 what? Could it be 12 metres, 12 centimetres?
Compare 12 cm with 12 m aloud and say why the unit changes what the number means.
Write the measurement with its unit (e.g. '12 cm', '3 kg') and read it aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: A bare number does not say how much; the unit is part of the measurement answer and changes its meaning entirely (12 cm vs 12 m).

activities.title: Name and touch the parts of a 3-D shape
feedback: If the child says 'corner' for vertex or 'side' for face, pair the correct term to the feature: edge is where two faces meet, vertex is a corner point, face is a flat surface.
If the child names a solid by one of its faces (e.g. calls a cube a 'square'), distinguish the whole solid from the flat square faces that make it up.
activities.rationale: EEF guidance recommends building precise mathematical vocabulary from informal to formal, attaching words to features through handling and talk. A rotatable on-screen 3-D model and a physical solid each help this spatial strand; a physical solid can be picked up and turned, while a screen model can be rotated and tapped to label — different experiences, neither uniquely necessary. Note this strand is spatial, whereas the equals-sign and units strands are not.
sourceClaims: Precise mathematical vocabulary should be built from informal to formal, with words attached to features (sides, corners) through handling and talk
learnerActions: Handle or rotate a 3-D solid (e.g. a cube-shaped block).
Point to and name each part: a face (a flat surface), an edge (where two faces meet), a vertex (a corner point).
Say which is which when asked to point to a face, an edge, and a vertex on the solid.
Use the precise words: say 'face' rather than 'side', learn 'vertex' as the mathematical name for a corner (corner is the everyday word), and do not call a cube a 'square'.
activities.intendedInsight: 3-D shapes have precise, named parts — face, edge, vertex — and a face is not the same as the 'side' of a flat shape; attaching the word to the felt feature is intended to help the vocabulary take hold.

activities.title: Convince the pedantic listener
feedback: If the child defends a running chain, have them restate what '=' promises and check both sides agree.
Prompt the child to say the sentence in words and confirm both sides are the same before the character accepts it.
activities.rationale: Valuing carefully formulated explanations — saying the sentence in words and checking both sides agree — supports MP6's emphasis on stating the meaning of symbols. A dialogue partner can draw out and repair imprecise statements; it is offered alongside, not instead of, the balance work, since talk may surface reasoning that a scored item does not.
sourceClaims: Proficient students state the meaning of the symbols they choose, using the equal sign consistently and appropriately, and are careful about specifying units of measure
learnerActions: Talk with an in-role character (e.g. a robot or shopkeeper) who reads notation literally and only accepts true, fully specified statements.
When the character asks 'you said 12 — 12 what?', supply the unit.
When the character asks 'is 7 + 5 really the same as 12 + 3?', state whether it is true and why.
Repair any imprecise statement so the literal-minded listener accepts it.
activities.intendedInsight: Precise symbol and unit use is what makes a statement unambiguous to a listener; explaining and repairing out loud may deepen the child's reasoning behind '=' and units.

activities.title: True/false and unit-completion screener
feedback: A wrong true/false verdict or a bare-number answer signals an operational reading of '=' or a dropped unit; follow with the balance task and the 'say it in words' discussion to surface the child's reasoning.
Use correct verdicts cautiously: the sorting items show the error pattern but do not by themselves reveal why the child thinks '=' means 'and then'.
activities.rationale: True/false number sentences and unit-completion items are natural scored checks that can screen the operational-equals error. Such a sorting check identifies the pattern but does not by itself surface the child's reasoning about why '=' means balance; it is positioned as a feeder into the balance and discussion activities.
sourceClaims: Most primary children interpret '=' operationally as 'the answer is', so few correctly complete 8+4=□+5 (they give 12 or 17); true/false and open number sentences build the relational 'is the same as' meaning
learnerActions: Sort number sentences as true or false, including items like 'is 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 true?'.
Complete 'add the unit' items where a bare number must be given its unit.
Flag any sentence that misuses '=' as a running total.
activities.intendedInsight: Quick true/false and unit items can reveal the operational-equals error and the missing-unit habit, signalling who needs the fuller balance and dialogue work.

constraints: The equals-sign strand is the priority: most primary children read '=' operationally, so teaching must directly confront the running-chain error with true/false and open sentences, not assume the relational meaning is obvious.
A true/false or unit-completion sorting check identifies the error pattern but does not itself elicit the child's reasoning or show why '=' means balance; pair it with discussion or balance work.

A labelled static picture or reference card can display finished, labelled examples but cannot let the child balance a sentence, attach a unit, or rotate a shape; use it only as a reference, not as the main learning mechanism.
The spatial 3-D shape strand (face/edge/vertex) benefits from a handled solid or rotatable model; the equals-sign and units strands are not spatial and need the balance and unit-naming work instead.

Physical solids have real thickness and can be picked up; an on-screen 3-D model is a rotatable representation. Both support the vocabulary strand through different experiences; neither is uniquely required. Do not teach 'can be picked up' as the test for a solid — ask instead about the mathematical shape and its named parts.
Recognition/sorting items alone do not elicit independent construction — have the child build balanced open sentences and state units themselves, not only pick from options.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit arithmetic: 7+5=12 and 12+3=15, so 7+5 (=12) does not equal 12+3 (=15); the chain 7+5=12+3=15 reaches the correct final total 15 but misuses '='. For 8+4=□+5: 8+4=12, so □=12-5=7. The distractors 12 (running total) and 17 (8+4+5) are documented wrong answers shown only as errors to diagnose, never as valid answers. The check 3+5=6+2 is a true sentence (both sides 8). These values are consistent throughout.

Balance-direction check: the original row stated the left pan (holding 12) 'sinks BELOW' the right pan (holding 15). This is physically reversed — the lighter 12-side rises and the heavier 15-side sinks. Activity 1 uses the correct direction; the original wording is recorded as an original-row error, not re-verified.

The source framed a static image as unable to teach and a quiz as unable to surface reasoning; these were softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements. A fixed labelled example can still teach as a reference, and scored items can be used during teaching as a screener.

The source links the operational-equals misconception to a prerequisite reteach topic, but that identifier is an internal reference not resolvable here; prerequisite reteaching is noted conceptually only.

The legacy fit rankings and the single preferred-artefact designation were dropped; the distinct pedagogical purposes of the balance, dialogue, 3-D model, and screener are preserved as separate activities rather than collapsed into one preferred format.
The comparison strand (greater than / less than; >, <, =) is retained in the summary but has no dedicated activity; it could be added if a fuller treatment of comparisons is wanted.

probeDeeper: Is 7 + 5 = 12 a true sentence? Is 7 + 5 = 12 + 3? What's the difference?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Justifying mathematical reasoning (age 8+)
topic.description: Construct and present multi-step mathematical arguments; critique the reasoning of others and explain clearly why a method works or fails
evidence: Explain why 1/3 > 1/5 using the idea that more parts means smaller pieces
Find and explain an error in a peer's column subtraction with exchanges
Present a chain of reasoning: since 6×8=48 and 6×2=12, then 6×10=60 so 6×8=60−12=48
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a classmate claims "you can't multiply a fraction and get a bigger answer", can {{name}} think through whether that's always true — and give an example to support or challenge the claim?

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9 the reasoning practice turns outward: children stop merely explaining their own method and begin CRITIQUING someone else's, and they string more than one fact into a chain ('since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48'). Two moves define the level — building a multi-step argument, and diagnosing why a peer's method fails, not just that its answer is wrong. This is the SMP3 'construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others' pairing made age-appropriate: arguments still lean on concrete referents (fraction bars, place-value equipment) but now demand a because/therefore link between steps. It is best taught not as a solo skill but through structured talk — analysing a deliberately flawed worked example, agreeing whether an argument 'makes sense', and being asked 'which STEP is wrong and why?' rather than 'is the answer right?'
bestPractices: Give children a peer's WRONG-but-plausible worked example (e.g. a column subtraction where the exchange was mis-recorded) and ask them to locate the faulty STEP and say why it breaks — not to redo it and compare answers
Model and require because/therefore connectives so a chain of facts becomes an argument ('since… and… therefore…'), scribing the child's spoken chain when their reasoning outruns their writing
Use 'convince me / convince a doubter' talk routines so an assertion is pushed into a justification; treat 'it just is' as the start, not the end
Anchor arguments in a shared representation (fraction bar, base-ten blocks) both parties can point at, so a critique targets the reasoning and not the person
Teach that finding one clear error and explaining it is worth more than re-solving — error analysis is the practice, per SMP3's 'distinguish correct logic from flawed logic and explain the flaw'
keyRepresentations: Fraction bars / area models for size arguments (more equal parts ⇒ smaller pieces, so 1/3 > 1/5)
Place-value equipment or a written column layout for locating an exchange error
A because/therefore sentence frame turning a list of facts into a chain
Derived-fact number strings (6×10, 6×2 ⇒ 6×8) shown as a linked sequence, not isolated facts
commonMisconceptions: 'It's wrong because the answer's different from mine' — judges a peer's argument by answer-agreement rather than by finding the flawed step
Checking one example and treating the rule as proved for all cases
Restating the method louder instead of giving a reason why it works
Believing a longer fraction/denominator names a bigger piece (1/5 > 1/3)

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, reasoning turns outward: children stop merely explaining their own method and begin critiquing someone else's, and they chain multiple facts into a single argument ('since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48'). Two moves define this level — building a multi-step because/therefore argument, and diagnosing WHY a peer's method fails (which step broke, not just that the answer differs). Arguments still lean on concrete referents (fraction bars, place-value equipment) but now require a because/therefore link between steps. Best taught through structured talk — analysing a deliberately flawed worked example, agreeing whether an argument 'makes sense', and asking 'which STEP is wrong and why?' rather than 'is the answer right?'

activities.title: Convince-me dialogue: catch the broken step
feedback: Name whether the faulty step was correctly located, not whether an answer matches: 'Yes — that flip is the broken line. Now tell me why flipping isn't allowed.'
If the child only announces the right answer ('it's 25'), redirect: 'Don't tell me the right answer yet — show me the first line where their thinking stops being okay, and say why that line breaks.'

If the child senses the error but cannot articulate it, revoice/scribe: offer 'you can't do that because…?' and let the child complete it; point at base-ten equipment so the reason has something to attach to. The reasoning is present even when the telling lags — do not treat this as not-knowing.

If the child agrees you can 'just do 6 take 1' because 'you always take the little one from the big one', this is a genuine false belief about the algorithm: build 71 with base-ten equipment, try to remove 6 ones, and force the exchange before returning to the argument skill.
activities.rationale: The level's core — constructing a chain and critiquing another's — is intrinsically dialogic. An in-role partner that asserts a flawed argument and asks the child to find and explain the broken step exercises SMP3's critique half, and 'how do you know?' pressure pushes the child's own assertions into because-clauses in real time. Children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so eliciting and scribing is appropriate rather than judging by fluency.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.

Reasoning develops along a describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder, and children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so a teacher must elicit and scribe the reasoning rather than judge it by fluency of telling.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a plausible-but-wrong worked chain, e.g. a partner says: 'I did 71 minus 46. I couldn't do 1 take 6, so I did 6 take 1, that's 5, then 7 take 4 is 3, so 35.'
Point to the EXACT line where the thinking first goes wrong (the digit-flip), rather than re-solving and comparing totals.
Say WHY that line breaks, grounded in place value: 'you can't flip the digits; the 1 is really part of 71, so you exchange a ten to make 11, and 11 take 6 is 5.'
When challenged with 'how do you know?' or 'why does exchanging fix it?', keep going until the objection becomes a because-chain.
Then construct a correct chain aloud for 71 − 46, starting from what 71 really is (giving 25).
activities.intendedInsight: Critiquing someone else's error forces your own reasoning to become explicit: a vague 'that's not right' can be turned, under questioning, into a because-chain you did not know you had.

activities.title: Build-an-argument workspace: chain the facts, mark the flaw
feedback: Report whether the flaw was correctly located, not whether a final answer matches.
If the child's chain lists facts without connectives, prompt: 'What word joins these two so the second follows from the first?'
If the marked step is wrong, ask the child to read each line aloud and test whether it genuinely follows from the one before.
activities.rationale: A build-an-argument workspace lets the child assemble a chain and mark the exact faulty step, making the 'which step, and why' move concrete and productive. Dragging/snapping tiles and tapping the broken step are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not required. This complements rather than replaces talk.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Assemble fact tiles ('6×10=60', '6×2=12') into a because/therefore sequence and write the linking reason, e.g. 'since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48.'
In a separate flawed worked example (a column subtraction with a mis-recorded exchange), tap or mark the single broken step and write or pick why it fails.
Check your own chain reads as 'since… and… therefore…', not just a list of true facts side by side.
activities.intendedInsight: A string of true facts only becomes an argument when because/therefore links them; locating 'which step, and why' is a concrete, repeatable move.

activities.title: Fraction-bar size argument: 1/3 > 1/5
feedback: Accept the chain only when it links the number of parts to the size of each part, not just 'the bar looks bigger'.
If the child believes a bigger denominator means a bigger piece, return to the shared bar split from the same whole and count/compare the actual pieces before re-stating the argument.
Treat 'it just is' as the start of a justification, not the end: ask 'convince a doubter'.
activities.rationale: Anchoring an argument in a shared representation lets a critique target the reasoning rather than the person, and directly addresses the common belief that a larger denominator names a bigger piece. For unit fractions the numerator is fixed at 1, so the comparison varies only the number of equal parts of the same whole. Concrete referents are age-appropriate for constructing arguments at this stage.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Using fraction bars or an area model showing the same whole split into 3 and into 5, state and justify which piece is bigger.
Build the chain: 'more equal parts means smaller pieces, so fifths are smaller than thirds, therefore 1/3 > 1/5.'
When a classmate claims '1/5 is bigger because 5 is bigger than 3', find and explain the flaw using the shared bar both of you can point at.
activities.intendedInsight: Splitting the same whole into MORE equal parts makes each part SMALLER, so a unit fraction with the larger denominator is the smaller number — and a representation both parties can point at keeps a critique about the reasoning, not the person.

activities.title: When is a check really a proof? Convince a doubter
feedback: Draw out that 'it works in one example' is evidence to explore, not a proof; ask what a doubter could still object to and what would be needed to be sure for every case.
For the inverse check, point out that 35 + 46 = 81, not 71 — so a careful exact check actually reveals 35 is wrong. 'Close to' only hints at plausibility; it does not prove the answer is right.
If the child treats one checked case as settling a general claim, offer a claim where a second case breaks it, and discuss what changed.
activities.rationale: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates at this age and the shift to deductive justification is slow and fragile; explicitly surfacing that checking examples does not prove a general claim targets a documented developmental step. The 'close to' inverse-check prompt extends this to verifying a single computation and is an agent-added illustration, conservatively framed as a proposal rather than a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates in this age range and the transition to deductive justification is slow and fragile; recognising that checking examples does not prove a general claim is a key developmental step.

Reasoning develops along a describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder, and children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so a teacher must elicit and scribe the reasoning rather than judge it by fluency of telling.
learnerActions: Given a general claim and a single example that fits it, decide whether checking that one example proves the claim for all cases.
Explain why one confirming example is not a proof, and what would be needed to be convinced for every case.
Evaluate a weak check such as: 'A classmate says 71 − 46 = 35 is fine because 35 + 46 is close to 71. Is that a good way to check? What does it actually tell you?'
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence that falls short of a complete argument — a single confirming example, or an approximate 'close to' check — does not establish or verify a claim; distinguishing 'it works here / it's roughly right' from 'it must always work / it is exactly right' is a key step toward justification.

activities.title: Compare-and-annotate launch: sound vs flawed argument
feedback: After the reveal, ask the child to re-explain the flaw without the annotation open.
Move promptly from recognising the flaw to constructing or critiquing a new one, so the productive half is exercised.
activities.rationale: A static correct-vs-flawed pair with tap-to-reveal annotations can seed critique and model reasons, but it shows arguments rather than eliciting the child's own chain or responding to their reasoning; treat it as a launch for talk, not as the assessment. Tap-to-reveal is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Study a side-by-side pair of worked arguments for the same problem — one sound, one with a hidden error.
Tap each step to reveal the reason it does or does not follow, then say in your own words which argument holds and where the other breaks.
Use this only as a springboard: afterwards, construct your OWN correct chain or critique a fresh flawed example aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a correct and a flawed argument side by side can seed critique and vocabulary for 'why a step follows', but reading annotations is only a starting point for producing your own argument.

constraints: The productive half of this practice — constructing a multi-step argument and explaining a flaw in the child's own words — requires construction and talk; a scored fixed-answer format can test RECOGNISING a correct argument or spotting a flagged flawed step, but a 'spot the flawed step' multiple-choice item should be used only as a warm-up and its score should not be treated as evidence of the reasoning practice.

Static compare-and-annotate pairs are scaffolds: they can show and label arguments but cannot elicit the child's own chain or respond to their reasoning. Follow them immediately with construction or critique.

Error analysis is the practice: finding one clear faulty step and explaining it is the goal, not re-solving and comparing answers. Keep critique pointed at the shared representation so it targets the reasoning, not the person.
Scribe/revoice a child whose reasoning outruns their words; do not judge reasoning by fluency of telling or score it.

Distinguish an argument-skill gap from a prerequisite gap: if a child endorses 'always take the smaller from the larger', reteach the column-subtraction exchange concept with base-ten equipment before expecting critique of that algorithm.

This guidance is medium-flexible: a live partner, scribed classroom talk, paper worked examples, or a screen workspace can all carry it. Interaction examples (tile snapping, tapping a step, tap-to-reveal) are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 71 − 46 = 25 (correct in the source). The flawed worked example's '35' is explicitly the peer's error to be critiqued, never presented as a valid answer. The exchange explanation (1 becomes 11, 11 − 6 = 5; tens become 6, 6 − 4 = 2, giving 25) is sound and preserved. Note also 35 + 46 = 81 ≠ 71, so the classmate's 'close to 71' inverse check would in fact expose the error; this is surfaced in the weak-evidence activity's feedback.

Self-audit of derived-fact chain: 6×8 = 60 − 12 = 48 is correct (6×10=60, 6×2=12). Note a wording inconsistency in the source: pedagogy and the first evidence item present the chain as 'since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48', but the third evidence item phrases it as 'since 6×8=48 and 6×2=12, then 6×10=60 so 6×8=60−12=48', which assumes the conclusion (6×8=48) as a premise — a circular/garbled ordering. Activities use the sound forward direction (6×10 and 6×2 ⇒ 6×8); the circular phrasing was not propagated.

Self-audit of fraction claim: 1/3 > 1/5 is correct and justified by more equal parts of the same whole meaning smaller pieces; both are unit fractions so only the number of parts varies. No 'denominator rule flips' language is used; same-whole scoping applies to comparing represented portions, while the fractions remain comparable as numbers.

The original labelled a conversation artefact 'ideal' and 3D 'poor/adds nothing'. Those are catalog fit rankings, not established pedagogical laws, and have been removed; the dialogic and workspace activities are presented as complementary options with stated affordances and limits rather than a universal 'only talk teaches this' claim.
Internal identifiers (microTopic and reteach-prerequisite IDs) were stripped from the guidance; the exchange prerequisite is retained conceptually only.

Activity 4 blends example-based generalisation (supported by Hoyles & Küchemann) with critique of an approximate single-computation 'close to' check; the 'close to' strand is an agent extension and is not directly supported by a cited source, though it is conservatively framed and its exact-check correction (35+46=81≠71) is mathematically sound.

probeDeeper: 'Show me the exact line where the thinking first goes wrong — put your finger on it.'
'Why can't you just swap it round and do 6 take away 1? What would you have to do instead?'
'A different classmate says 71 − 46 = 35 is fine because 35 + 46 is close to 71. Is that a good way to check? What does it actually tell you?'
'Now build me a correct chain for 71 − 46 out loud — start with what 71 really is.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child locating the specific faulty STEP (flipping 1−6 into 6−1 instead of exchanging a ten) AND giving a reason grounded in place value (the 1 is part of 71, so you take a ten to make 11, then 11−6=5), rather than just announcing that 35 is the wrong answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges the peer's argument by answer-agreement, not by the reasoning: 'it's wrong because I got 25' — re-solves and compares totals without ever locating or explaining the faulty step.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect from answer to step: 'Don't tell me the right answer yet — show me the first line where their thinking stops being okay, and say why that line breaks.' Model once on a different flawed example.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child announces the correct answer or redoes the calculation but cannot point to WHICH step is wrong or WHY; treats 'different answer' as the whole critique.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts the smaller-from-larger step as fine — shares the bug: agrees you can 'just do 6 take 1' because 'you always take the little one from the big one.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a genuine false belief about the algorithm — confront it with base-ten equipment: build 71, try to remove 6 ones, force the exchange. Reteach the exchange concept, not the argument skill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses the flipped subtraction, or hesitates only about the final total, treating column subtraction as digit-by-digit with the smaller digit always subtracted.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees something is wrong and objects, but the objection stays at 'that's not right' — reasoning outruns communication, no because-clause emerges even though the child clearly senses the flaw.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as not-knowing. Scribe/revoice: offer 'you can't do that because…?' and let the child complete it; point at base-ten blocks so the reason has something to attach to. The reasoning is present; only the telling lags.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Frowns, says 'no you can't do that' or 'it doesn't work like that' but cannot yet articulate the place-value reason when asked 'why not?'

responseLevels.gap: Only evaluates the answer ('it's 25, so they're wrong') or redoes the sum; cannot locate the faulty step or gives no reason.
responseLevels.full: Pinpoints the flipped-subtraction step AND explains the place-value reason it fails (the 1 stands for part of 71, so a ten must be exchanged to make 11−6=5), then reconstructs a correct because/therefore chain — and transfers the 'find the broken step and say why' move to a new flawed example unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Locates the wrong step (the digit-flip) but explains it as 'that's not the rule' or restates the correct procedure without the place-value reason; can describe the steps but not why the flawed one breaks.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is how a classmate worked out 71 − 46. They wrote: '1 take away 6 — I can't, so I'll do 6 take away 1, that's 5. Then 7 take away 4 is 3. So the answer is 35.' Is their thinking okay? Talk me through what they did, step by step, and tell me where — if anywhere — it goes wrong and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who genuinely constructs and critiques arguments identifies the exact broken step and explains the place-value reason it fails; a child who only checks answers will say 'it's wrong, it should be 25' (or redo the sum) without ever naming which step broke or why — same surface verdict, completely different reasoning. Because the error is a real, well-documented one (the 'always take smaller from larger' / smaller-from-larger bug), a child reasoning correctly and one reasoning by answer-agreement give observably different responses.

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9 precision spans fraction/decimal vocabulary, naming angle types (acute, obtuse) accurately, specifying units in measurement and money, and using notation (=, <, >, ÷, ×) correctly. Two strands become load-bearing: area answers need a SQUARE unit ('63 square centimetres', not '63' or '63 cm', because area counts unit squares), and time in 24-hour notation (15:45) must be kept distinct from 12-hour am/pm ('15:45 pm' is a contradiction). Following EEF's KS2 guidance, the teacher rephrases vague pupil language into precise mathematical language rather than merely marking it wrong.
bestPractices: Tie the unit to what is being measured — area counts squares, so it is cm²; contrast 63 cm (a length) with 63 cm² (an area) so the unit carries meaning (CCSS: specify units)
Keep number systems distinct: 24-hour time (00:00–23:59) has no am/pm; show 15:45 and 3:45 pm as the same moment via subtracting 12
Name angles against a right angle — acute is smaller, obtuse is larger — rather than 'big/small angle' (CCSS: clear vocabulary)
Rephrase vague responses into precise mathematical language, modelling the correct term rather than only correcting (EEF KS2/3)
Read notation aloud and have pupils explain, so terms and symbols stay linked to meaning

Dual 24-hour / 12-hour clock display
Angles compared to a right-angle template (acute/obtuse)

commonMisconceptions: Gives an area with no unit or a length unit — '63' or '63 cm' instead of '63 cm²'
Mixes 24-hour and 12-hour notation — writes '15:45 pm', or cannot relate 15:45 to 3:45 pm
Names angle types imprecisely — swaps acute and obtuse, or says 'big angle'
Treats 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' as different amounts rather than two correct names for the same value

learn.summary: Mathematical precision for ages 8-9: tie units to what is measured (area counts unit squares, so it is cm², not a bare number or a length unit), keep 24-hour time distinct from 12-hour am/pm (15:45 is the same moment as 3:45 pm, but '15:45 pm' is a contradiction), name angle types against a right angle (acute smaller, obtuse larger and less than a straight angle), and treat 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' as two names for the same value. The teaching move throughout is to rephrase vague language into precise mathematical language and ask the child to say why the exact unit or notation matters, rather than only marking an answer wrong.

activities.title: Tiling to find the unit for area
feedback: If the child writes '63' with no unit, ask: '63 what? Is 63 cm the same as 63 cm²?' and point to the tiled squares.
If the child writes '63 cm', show that cm measures a length along an edge, while the squares filling the rectangle each cover an area, so the count of squares is cm².
When the child supplies '63 cm²' and explains it counts unit squares, confirm that the unit now carries the meaning of the answer.
activities.rationale: Letting the child see area built from counting unit squares makes the square unit come from the structure of the quantity rather than being an arbitrary label; EEF advises rephrasing vague responses into precise mathematical language and using contrasting non-examples (63 cm vs 63 cm²).

Teachers should support pupils to use language reflecting mathematical structure by rephrasing vague, non-mathematical responses into appropriate mathematical language, and address misconceptions with counterexamples and non-examples
learnerActions: Enter or write the area of a rectangle, e.g. '63'.
Fill (or draw) the rectangle with unit squares that tile it exactly, counting the squares.
Revise the answer to carry a square unit: '63 cm²' or '63 square centimetres'.
Contrast an edge length of 63 cm (a length measured along one side) with an area of 63 cm² (unit squares covering the inside), and say why they are different quantities.
Answer the prompt: 'why does the unit have to be square?'
activities.intendedInsight: Area counts how many unit squares cover a region, so its unit is a square unit (cm²); a bare number says how many but not of what, and a plain length unit (cm) describes a distance, not a covering.

activities.title: One moment, two clocks: 24-hour vs am/pm
feedback: If the child writes '15:45 pm', ask: 'What does the pm add, or clash with? Does 24-hour time use am/pm?'
If the child cannot relate 15:45 to 3:45 pm, model the subtraction 15 − 12 = 3 and show both naming the same instant.
Confirm success when the child keeps the systems separate and converts between them fluently with a reason.
activities.rationale: Showing the same instant two ways makes the contradiction in '15:45 pm' concrete and gives a conversion method for afternoon and evening times (subtract 12 for 13:00–23:59), with the noon and midnight hours handled separately; this reflects attending to precision in notation.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, use clear definitions and vocabulary, and state the meaning of the symbols they use to communicate precisely
learnerActions: Read a time written in 24-hour notation, e.g. 15:45.

Convert it to 12-hour am/pm: for times from 13:00 to 23:59, subtract 12 from the hour and write pm (15 − 12 = 3, giving 3:45 pm); 12:00–12:59 stays 12 and is pm, 00:00–00:59 becomes 12 am, and 01:00–11:59 keep their hour and are am. Check both show the same moment on a dual clock display.
Decide whether '15:45 pm' can be correct, and explain what the 'pm' clashes with.
Write the same time correctly in each system and state that 24-hour time runs 00:00–23:59 with no am/pm.
activities.intendedInsight: 24-hour and 12-hour are two complete, separate ways of naming the same moment; 'pm' belongs only to the 12-hour system, so stamping it onto a 24-hour time mixes two systems and contradicts itself.

activities.title: Naming angles against a right angle
feedback: If the child says 'big angle' or 'small angle', ask them to compare it to a right angle and attach the term acute or obtuse to that comparison.
If acute and obtuse are swapped, re-anchor on the right-angle template: acute is smaller, obtuse is larger.
Confirm when the child names the type and can say how they are sure.
activities.rationale: Anchoring vocabulary to a right-angle comparison replaces vague size words with a precise, checkable criterion, consistent with using clear mathematical vocabulary.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, use clear definitions and vocabulary, and state the meaning of the symbols they use to communicate precisely
learnerActions: Place or overlay a right-angle template on a given angle.
Decide whether the angle is smaller than a right angle (acute), exactly a right angle (right angle), or larger than a right angle but less than a straight angle (obtuse).
State the angle type using the correct term and justify it by the comparison, avoiding 'big angle' or 'small angle'.
Repeat for several angles, including some close to a right angle.
activities.intendedInsight: Angle names are defined by comparison to a right angle (acute < right < obtuse), so the right angle is the reference that makes the vocabulary precise and reliable.

activities.title: Two names, one value: fraction vocabulary
feedback: If the child treats 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' as different, show both pointing to the same ¾ and the same shaded region.
When the child reads a symbol aloud and explains its meaning, confirm the term and symbol are linked to meaning.
activities.rationale: Linking words, symbols and meaning keeps notation tied to understanding; reading aloud and explaining supports precise mathematical language.

Teachers should support pupils to use language reflecting mathematical structure by rephrasing vague, non-mathematical responses into appropriate mathematical language, and address misconceptions with counterexamples and non-examples
learnerActions: Match fraction words to symbols, e.g. 'three quarters' = 'three fourths' = ¾.
Explain that 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' name the same amount, not two different amounts.
Read notation aloud (=, <, >, ÷, ×) and state what each symbol means in a given statement.
activities.intendedInsight: A value can have more than one correct name; 'quarter' and 'fourth' are two words for the same part, and symbols carry fixed meanings that should be read and explained, not just copied.

activities.title: In-role questioner who takes answers literally
feedback: The character should accept an answer only once the unit or notation is unambiguous, prompting 'specify and repair' until it is.
If the child repairs without reason, ask them to say what the original was missing.
activities.rationale: Dialogue that queries bare numbers and mixed time systems draws out the precise unit and notation and lets the child practise repairing their own language, matching EEF's rephrasing-into-precise-language guidance. Offered as an alternative route; this is a proposal, not a claim that dialogue is required or superior to other media.
sourceClaims: Teachers should support pupils to use language reflecting mathematical structure by rephrasing vague, non-mathematical responses into appropriate mathematical language, and address misconceptions with counterexamples and non-examples
learnerActions: Give answers to a character (e.g. a robot or timetable clerk) who queries anything imprecise: '63 what — is that a length or an area?', 'you can't put pm on a 24-hour time'.
Specify the missing unit or repair the mixed notation in response to each query.
State in your own words why the correction matters.
activities.intendedInsight: Precision is what lets another reader interpret an answer correctly; a bare number or mixed notation leaves the meaning ambiguous.

activities.title: Fix-the-notation screener
feedback: Correct responses supply the square unit and spot the 24-hour/pm contradiction; use misses to route the child to the tiling or dual-clock activity.
Because recognition and completion items confirm the fix but not the reasoning, follow up by asking the child to explain why.
activities.rationale: Short items screen efficiently for the units slip and 24-hour errors, but a screener on its own checks the correction rather than eliciting the reasoning behind the convention, so it is best used to feed the richer activities.
learnerActions: Complete items that add the missing unit to an answer (e.g. turn '63' into '63 cm²').
Convert between 24-hour and am/pm (e.g. 15:45 ↔ 3:45 pm) and flag a mixed form like '15:45 pm' as wrong.
Identify a diagnostic case: 'A child wrote the area as 63 and a time as 15:45 pm — fix anything that isn't right and say why the missing or wrong part matters.'
activities.intendedInsight: Quick items can reveal who leaves units off or mixes time systems, pointing to where fuller teaching is needed.

constraints: Area answers must carry a square unit (cm²/square centimetres): a bare number or a length unit (cm) is not an acceptable area, because area counts unit squares.
24-hour time runs 00:00–23:59 and uses no am/pm; '15:45 pm' is a contradiction and must be either 15:45 or 3:45 pm.
Angle names are defined relative to a right angle (acute < right < obtuse, with obtuse less than a straight angle); 'big'/'small angle' is not precise naming.

A static labelled reference can show correct units and time formats but does not itself let the child tile an area, convert a time, or repair notation, so pair any reference with activities that require the child to produce and correct.
Recognition/completion items confirm whether a fix is applied but do not on their own elicit the child's explanation of why the convention matters; follow them with a 'say why' prompt.

Interactive feedback examples (a rectangle that fills with unit squares, a dual clock lighting 15:45 and 3:45 pm together, an error on '15:45 pm', a right-angle overlay) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory tooling; the same insights can be reached with paper tiling, drawn clocks, and a paper right-angle corner.
