pedagogy.summary: At 9-10 precision covers number vocabulary (prime, factor, multiple), polygon regularity, units including cm², m³ and degrees, and index/percentage notation. Two confusions are load-bearing: factor versus multiple (a factor divides INTO a number; a multiple is built by multiplying it), and reading index notation — 5² is 'five squared' (5×5 = 25), not 'five times two'. Precision also means matching the unit's dimension to the quantity (cm² for area, cm³ for volume) and marking an estimate as approximate ('approximately 60 cm³') rather than presenting it as exact. Teaching rephrases vague language into structural terms (EEF).
bestPractices: Distinguish factor and multiple with arrays and factor pairs — a factor fits into the number, a multiple is a step in its times-table — and rephrase pupils' loose usage into the precise term (EEF)
Teach 5² as a square of side 5 (5×5) and read it 'five squared', contrasting it directly with 5×2 to break the index-as-multiplier error (CCSS: state the meaning of symbols)
Match the unit to the dimension: area counts squares (cm²), volume fills cubes (cm³); make the little index meaningful
Mark estimates as approximate, expressing answers to a precision appropriate for the context (CCSS)
Use non-examples and counterexamples to test a definition (is 1 prime? is 6 a factor of 12?) (EEF)

A square of dots for n² and a cube for n³
Unit-square (cm²) and unit-cube (cm³) diagrams
Regular vs irregular polygons side by side
Notation cards linking symbol, word and value (5² = 'five squared' = 25)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses factor and multiple, using them interchangeably or in the wrong direction ('6 is a multiple of 12')
Reads index notation as multiplication by the index — 5² as 5×2 = 10
Uses cm for an area or volume, or writes cm² where cm³ is needed
Presents an estimate as an exact value, omitting 'approximately'

learn.summary: Builds precise mathematical vocabulary and notation for 9-10 year olds: distinguishing factor from multiple, reading index notation (5² = 'five squared' = 5×5 = 25, not 5×2), matching units to dimension (cm² for area, cm³ for volume), and marking estimates as approximate. Core approach: let children test definitions with arrays and dot-squares, rephrase loose language into structural terms, and justify each convention. Two load-bearing confusions are targeted: factor vs multiple (a factor divides INTO a number; a multiple is built FROM it by multiplying) and the index-as-multiplier misread.

activities.title: Testing factor vs multiple with arrays
feedback: If a learner says '6 is a multiple of 12', ask them to build 6 by counting up in 12s; when that fails, ask whether 6 fits into a 12-array. The array shows factor; the times-table step shows multiple.
If they state the relationship backwards or cannot say which term applies, rephrase their loose usage into the precise term and re-test with the arrays before moving on.

Reinforce by testing the definition with both examples and non-examples: is 6 a factor of 12 (yes)? is 5 a factor of 12 (no — 12 ÷ 5 leaves a remainder)? is 1 prime (no — a prime has exactly two different factors, and 1 has only one)? Let them test rather than recall.
activities.rationale: Arrays and factor pairs make the divides-into vs built-from distinction concrete and testable; rephrasing vague usage into structural terms and probing definitions with non-examples/counterexamples follows EEF guidance on vocabulary and misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Teachers should rephrase pupils' vague, non-mathematical language into language reflecting mathematical structure, and address misconceptions by exploring their partial truth and using counterexamples and non-examples
learnerActions: Take the statement '6 is a multiple of 12' and test it: try to build 6 by stepping up in 12s (12, 24, 36...) — it never lands on 6.
Now test whether 6 fits INTO a 12-array (arrange 12 as two rows of 6, or six columns of 2) — it does, evenly.
State the corrected sentence: '6 is a FACTOR of 12' (equivalently, '12 is a multiple of 6'), and say why.
Repeat with a second pair: is 24 a factor or a multiple of 12? Build it by stepping up in 12s (12, 24) to show it is a multiple.
Write the definition in your own words: a factor fits into a number exactly, with no remainder; a multiple is a step in that number's times-table.
activities.intendedInsight: A factor divides evenly INTO a number, while a multiple is built FROM it by multiplying — so direction matters and the terms are not interchangeable.

activities.title: Drawing 5² to break the index-as-multiplier error
feedback: If a learner reads 5² as 'five times two' or '10', have them draw the 5×5 square and count the dots, then place the 5×2 strip of 10 next to it to see the gap.
Insist on the spoken form 'five squared' and ask them to state what the symbol means, linking symbol, word and value (5² = 'five squared' = 25).
If they transfer the error to 5³, build it as a cube (5×5×5 = 125) so 'cubed' is visible.
activities.rationale: Representing n² as a square of dots directly contrasts the correct value with the 5×2 misread, and stating the meaning of the symbol aloud supports precise notation use (CCSS MP6).
sourceClaims: Proficient students use clear definitions and vocabulary, state the meaning of symbols, specify units, and express answers to a degree of precision appropriate to the context (including marking estimates)
learnerActions: Draw 5² as a square of dots, 5 across and 5 down, and count them: 25.
Right beside it, draw 5×2 as a strip of 10 dots.
Say each aloud: '5 squared is 5×5 = 25' and '5 times 2 is 10' — notice they are different.
Explain in words why 5² means a square of side 5, not 'five times two'.
Extend: sketch what 5³ would mean (a cube, 5×5×5 = 125) and read it 'five cubed'.
activities.intendedInsight: The small raised index counts how many copies of the base are multiplied together — two for a square (5²=5×5=25), three for a cube (5³=5×5×5=125) — so the index is not a multiplier, and 5² is 25, not 10.

activities.title: Matching units to dimension and marking estimates
feedback: If a learner writes cm for an area or volume, have them count the squares or cubes and ask which index records what they counted.
If they give an estimated volume as an exact figure, ask how a reader would know it was an estimate; prompt the 'approximately' tag.
Connect back to notation: the little number on cm² is the same squaring idea as the index on 5² — cm² is cm×cm, so it records a dimension.
activities.rationale: Using unit-square and unit-cube models grounds the dimension-matching convention, and expressing answers to a precision appropriate to context (including marking estimates) is an explicit precision practice (CCSS MP6).
sourceClaims: Proficient students use clear definitions and vocabulary, state the meaning of symbols, specify units, and express answers to a degree of precision appropriate to the context (including marking estimates)
learnerActions: Cover a flat shape with 1 cm by 1 cm unit squares and write its area with cm² — the little ² records that you counted square centimetres.
Fill a box with 1 cm unit cubes and write its volume with cm³ — the ³ records that you filled cubic centimetres.
Given an estimated volume of about 60 cm³, write it as 'approximately 60 cm³' rather than '60 cm³', and say why the word matters.
Spot and fix errors: correct '48' (an area measured in square centimetres) to '48 cm²', and correct an estimate written as an exact figure by adding 'approximately'.
Explain what the index on the unit tells you about the dimension being measured.
activities.intendedInsight: The unit's index matches the dimension measured — area counts squares (cm²), volume fills cubes (cm³) — and an estimate must be flagged 'approximately' so it is not read as exact.

activities.title: Spot-the-error diagnostic dialogue
feedback: Listen for the correction of '6 is a multiple of 12' to '6 is a FACTOR of 12' (or '12 is a multiple of 6') WITH the reason that a factor divides into a number while a multiple is what you get by multiplying it.
Listen for 5² read as 'five squared' = 5×5 = 25, not 5×2; if the learner accepts the wrong statements, reteach using the array and dot-square activities.
An in-role mathematician who insists on the right term and challenges a misread can surface the vocabulary through dialogue, prompting the child to correct and justify rather than simply be told.
activities.rationale: A dialogue that rephrases loose language into structural terms and challenges a misread can elicit the learner's own reasoning about definitions; recognition-only sort/label items do not themselves elicit that explanation or the independent production of the corrected term. Surfaced for discussion, not scored.
sourceClaims: Teachers should rephrase pupils' vague, non-mathematical language into language reflecting mathematical structure, and address misconceptions by exploring their partial truth and using counterexamples and non-examples
learnerActions: Read two statements written by another child: '6 is a multiple of 12' and '5² is five times two, which is 10'.
Decide whether each is right or wrong.
Fix each one and explain the difference that makes the original wrong.
Respond when a partner (or teacher in role) pushes back — 'did you mean factor or multiple?', 'read that power aloud' — and justify your correction.
Answer the follow-ups: Is 24 a factor or a multiple of 12? Why is a volume in cm³ and an area in cm²?
activities.intendedInsight: Both wrong statements look plausible; precision means catching the definite reason each is wrong — the factor/multiple direction and the meaning of the squared symbol — and justifying the fix.

constraints: Sort/label and 'read the notation' screener items can efficiently flag factor/multiple and index errors, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the child's reasoning about the definitions or independent construction of the corrected term — pair any screener with a task requiring the learner to explain or produce.
A static reference card of terms and notation can support recall, but does not let the child test a definition or produce notation; treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main activity.

A unit-cube model is useful for grounding 'cubed' and cm³, which is genuinely spatial; factor/multiple and most of this band are not spatial, so a 3D model is a companion for the volume-notation strand only, not a general requirement.
Drawn dot-squares and unit-square/cube diagrams are concrete approximations; distinguish the counted squares/cubes from the quantity (area/volume) they represent.
Estimate-tagging ('approximately') depends on the task being genuinely an estimate — do not apply it to exact measured or computed values.

topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes up maths involving algebra or 3-D shapes, do they use precise language — like "algebraic expression", "cubic centimetres", or "coordinates" — and apply the correct notation throughout?

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11, the capstone, precision covers the vocabulary of ratio, proportion, algebra, volume, coordinate geometry and circle parts, plus algebraic notation and order of operations. Two distinctions are load-bearing: the parts of a circle (radius is centre-to-circumference, diameter is all the way across = twice the radius, circumference is the distance around), and the difference between an expression, an equation and a formula (an expression has no equals sign; an equation asserts two things are equal; a formula is a general rule relating quantities). Following EEF, pupils should read expressions as descriptions of relationships, not just instructions to calculate, and use precise terms that reflect structure.
bestPractices: Sort algebraic objects into expression / equation / formula by their defining feature — the presence and role of '=' — and read expressions as relationships, not just 'work it out' (EEF; CCSS)
Label a circle so radius, diameter and circumference attach to features, and establish diameter = 2 × radius
Match volume units to the quantity (cm³ fills space) and keep them distinct from area (cm²)
Rephrase informal responses into precise mathematical language, choosing the formal register (EEF; the cross-curricular formal-vocabulary link)
Test definitions with non-examples — 'is 3x + 5 an equation?' — to sharpen the boundaries (EEF)
keyRepresentations: A labelled circle (radius, diameter, circumference) with diameter = 2r shown
Sorting cards: expression (3x+5) vs equation (3x+5=11) vs formula (V=l×w×h)
Unit-cube model for volume (cm³)
Ratio/proportion notation (a : b) with a bar or double number line
Order-of-operations worked expressions read as relationships
commonMisconceptions: Conflates expression, equation and formula — calls 3x + 5 an equation, or uses the terms interchangeably
Confuses circle parts — says the diameter is centre-to-edge (that is the radius), or calls the circumference the 'edge'/'side'
Omits the volume unit or uses the wrong dimension — '60' or '60 cm²' instead of '60 cm³'
Reads an algebraic expression only as an instruction to calculate rather than a relationship, mishandling order of operations

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, this capstone strand builds precise mathematical vocabulary and notation: distinguishing an expression (no equals sign; it can be evaluated or simplified but not solved) from an equation (asserts two things are equal; an equation such as 3x + 5 = 11 can be solved) from a formula (a special kind of equation that states a general rule relating quantities); naming circle parts correctly (radius = centre to circumference, diameter = all the way across through the centre = 2 × radius, circumference = the distance around); and attaching the right units to a quantity (volume in cm³, distinct from area in cm²). Following EEF, learners should read expressions as descriptions of relationships, not just instructions to calculate, and use terms that reflect mathematical structure.

activities.title: Sort algebra cards by the role of '='
feedback: If a learner labels '3x + 5' an equation, ask them to point to the equals sign — there is none, so it is an expression you can evaluate (for a given x) or simplify, but not solve.
If a learner cannot separate equation from formula, contrast '3x + 5 = 11' (a claim true for one value of x, which you solve) with 'V = l × w × h' (a general rule true for any box, which you use).
Praise a learner who names the defining feature spontaneously rather than guessing from the look of the symbols.
If a learner reads '3x + 5' only as 'multiply x by 3 and add 5', prompt them to also describe it as a relationship: '5 more than three times a number'.
activities.rationale: Sorting and justifying by a single defining feature sharpens the boundary between easily-confused terms, and reading expressions as relationships rather than instructions follows EEF guidance. An optional interactive sorting tool can highlight or colour the '=' in the last two cards as the learner sorts, making the defining feature visible, but the sorting and verbal justification carry the learning.

learnerActions: Sort three cards — '3x + 5', '3x + 5 = 11', 'V = l × w × h' — into three bins labelled expression, equation and formula.

For each card, say out loud what makes it belong there: Does it have an equals sign? If it does, is it a statement of equality that is true only for particular values of an unknown (one you solve), or a general rule relating quantities that holds for any values (a formula, which is a special kind of equation)?

Explain the consequence: an expression can be evaluated (worked out once you know the value of the letter) or simplified, but not solved, while an equation like 3x + 5 = 11 can be solved (find the unknown that makes it true).
Test the boundary with a non-example question such as 'Is 3x + 5 an equation? Why not?' and 'What single change would turn 3x + 5 into an equation?'
activities.intendedInsight: The presence and role of '=' is the defining feature: an expression has none, an equation like 3x + 5 = 11 asserts equality for a particular unknown value (and can be solved), and a formula is a special kind of equation that states a general rule relating quantities for any values. The precise term changes what you are allowed to do with the object.

activities.title: Build the radius–diameter–circumference relationship on a circle
feedback: If a learner says the diameter is centre-to-edge, name that as the radius and have them re-mark the diameter all the way across through the centre.
If a learner calls the circumference the 'edge' or 'side', supply the precise term and tie it to 'the distance all the way around'.
Reinforce when a learner states diameter = 2 × radius and can explain why confusing the two matters.
activities.rationale: Attaching precise terms to features of a manipulated or drawn circle makes the relationship felt rather than memorised. An optional live diagram where dragging the radius auto-draws the diameter at twice its length and traces the circumference makes the 2× relationship dynamic; a drawn or physical circle achieves the same with manual marking.
sourceClaims: Proficient students communicate precisely with clear definitions, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and specify units of measure
learnerActions: On a labelled circle, point to and name the radius, the diameter and the circumference in your own words.
State how the radius and diameter are related and justify it: the diameter goes all the way across through the centre and is exactly twice the radius.
Using a drawn or physical circle, mark a radius, then mark the diameter as two radii end-to-end through the centre, then trace the full distance around for the circumference.

Catch a deliberate error: respond to 'the diameter is the distance from the centre to the edge' by correcting it (that is the radius) and explaining what difference the correction makes to any calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: Radius, diameter and circumference name distinct features that stand in a fixed relationship (diameter = 2 × radius), so the words are not interchangeable; swapping radius and diameter gives a wrong answer. For a length such as the circumference it halves or doubles the answer, and for an area it multiplies or divides the answer by 4.

activities.title: Attach the right unit to volume
feedback: If a learner writes just '60', ask '60 what?' and have them add the unit.
If a learner writes '60 cm²' for a volume, point out that cm² measures area (a surface); filling space needs cm³.
Confirm when a learner both gives the correct cubic unit and can say why space-filling means cubic.
activities.rationale: Grounding 'cubed' in a unit-cube model connects the exponent to physically filling space, and insisting on the unit follows the precision standard. The spatial unit-cube model is the one genuinely three-dimensional strand here.
sourceClaims: Proficient students communicate precisely with clear definitions, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and specify units of measure
learnerActions: Work out the volume of a box (e.g. with a unit-cube model, counting how many 1 cm cubes fill it) and write the answer with its unit.
State why the unit is cm³ and not cm² or a bare number: volume fills space in three dimensions, so it is counted in cubic units.
Contrast a volume (cm³) with an area (cm²) for the same figure, saying what each measures.
activities.intendedInsight: A quantity is incomplete without its unit, and the unit must match the dimension: volume fills space so it is measured in cubic units (cm³), distinct from area's square units (cm²).

activities.title: Expert dialogue: justify the precise term
feedback: When a learner slips (expression called an equation, radius called diameter), the questioner asks them to justify, prompting self-correction rather than supplying the answer.
Rephrase a learner's informal response ('the line across') into the formal register ('the diameter') and ask them to reuse it.
activities.rationale: Dialogue that demands justification surfaces the reasoning behind the vocabulary, which sorting alone may not elicit. Rephrasing informal talk into the formal register follows EEF guidance. This complements, rather than replaces, hands-on sorting and manipulation.
sourceClaims: Teachers should rephrase vague responses into language reflecting mathematical structure and encourage pupils to read numerical and algebraic expressions as descriptions of relationships rather than merely instructions to calculate
learnerActions: Respond to an in-role questioner who insists on the exact term: 'Is that an expression or an equation? What makes it one?'
When you use loose language, restate it in precise mathematical terms when asked.
Defend your classification or your circle-part naming with the defining feature, not just the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to name the defining reason — the role of the equals sign, centre-to-edge versus all-the-way-across — is what distinguishes precise understanding from loose usage.

constraints: A sort-and-label task can check whether a learner picks the right category or label efficiently, but on its own it does not surface the reasoning that defines the terms; pair it with a task or dialogue that asks 'what makes it one?'.
A static labelled diagram or definition list is a useful reference, but it does not let the learner sort, manipulate or justify, so it cannot by itself build the distinctions.
Recognition-only responses (choosing the right label) do not elicit independent construction of a definition; include tasks where the learner states the defining feature in their own words.

A physical unit-cube model or paper circle has real thickness and can be handled; treat it as an approximation to the idealised mathematical figure (which has exact faces/edges or zero thickness) when discussing area versus volume.

Optional interactive features (auto-drawing the diameter at 2× the radius, highlighting the '=', tracing the circumference) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory; a drawn or physical circle and card sorting work equally well.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: diameter = 2 × radius, centre-to-circumference radius, circumference as distance around, and volume in cm³ versus area in cm² are all internally consistent and correct as stated in the source. No arithmetic or conceptual errors were found to correct.

The original source asserted that a static image 'cannot' teach and that a quiz 'cannot surface the reasoning'; these have been softened to narrowly scoped limits (reference-only vs. construction-eliciting) rather than universal claims about media.

The source's '60 cm³' volume task does not specify the box dimensions; the rewritten activity frames it generically (count unit cubes) and uses 60 only to illustrate bare-number versus unit, so no unverified arithmetic is asserted.

Residual catalog/product vocabulary ('bench', 'screener') is absent from the final learner-facing guidance; a fresh scan confirms no artefactType labels, fit rankings, 'recommended' or quiz-step terms remain.

topic.name: Constructing mathematical arguments
topic.description: Construct and present logical mathematical arguments involving multiple steps and formal reasoning; critique others' reasoning about fractions, algebra, ratio, or geometry and clearly explain errors or alternative approaches
evidence: Prove that a given angle must be 60° by chaining angle facts in a logical sequence
Find and explain the error in a peer's fraction division calculation
Construct a counter-example to disprove a false conjecture (e.g. 'multiplying always makes bigger')
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} presents a multi-step maths solution, do they lay out their reasoning clearly enough that someone else could follow every step — and can they spot the flaw if a worked solution contains a logical error?

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 the reasoning practice reaches its primary-school ceiling: formal, multi-step arguments and their sharpest tool, the counter-example. A child chains angle facts to PROVE a given angle must be 60° (not measure it), finds and explains an error in a peer's fraction division, and — the signature move — disproves a false conjecture such as 'multiplying always makes bigger' with a single case (×1/2 makes smaller). This is where the empirical→deductive asymmetry Hoyles & Küchemann document becomes explicit content: one counter-example kills a universal claim, while no number of confirming examples establishes it. SMP3's critique half is now central — arguments span fractions, ratio, algebra and geometry, and a competent Y6 reasoner locates a flawed step, explains why it fails, and offers a correct alternative. Teaching aims at the felt logic of implication: 'if… then…', the difference between a claim and its converse, and why a counter-example is decisive.
bestPractices: Make the counter-example a taught tool: give false 'always/sometimes/never' conjectures ('multiplying makes bigger', 'the more sides, the bigger the angles') and reward the single case that breaks them, per Hoyles & Küchemann's finding that a counter-example reveals WHY a claim is false

Require proof by chained fact, not measurement: to show an angle is 60°, insist on a logical progression of angle facts ('angles on a line sum to 180°, and these two are 60° and 60°, therefore…'), reserving measuring for checking

Use peer critique across arenas — a flawed fraction division ('invert the first fraction'), a mis-added ratio, a misaligned calculation — and demand 'which step, why, and what's the correct method' (SMP3 explain-the-flaw plus alternative)
Draw the claim/converse distinction with concrete cases so 'if it's a square then it has four right angles' is not confused with its converse
Keep pressing convince→justify: a confident explanation that has gaps is convincing; a correct, complete because/therefore chain is justifying — name which one the child has produced
keyRepresentations: A single well-chosen counter-example as a disproof object (e.g. 6 × 1/2 = 3 against 'multiplying makes bigger')
Chained angle-fact diagrams (angles on a line / in a triangle / vertically opposite) building to a proved value
Scaling picture of multiplication (× less than 1 shrinks, × 1 keeps, × more than 1 grows) to reason about product size without computing
A because/therefore proof frame linking givens through steps to conclusion
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplication always makes bigger / division always makes smaller' — the whole-number generalisation that fails for factors below 1
Confirming a conjecture with examples and calling it proved (empirical proof scheme)
Confusing a statement with its converse ('if square then 4 right angles' ⇒ 'if 4 right angles then square')
Inverting the wrong fraction in division, or 'dividing straight across', and critiquing only by the odd-looking answer rather than the faulty step
Believing a proved geometric result holds only for the specific diagram drawn

learn.summary: For 10-11 year-olds, this builds formal, multi-step mathematical argument and its critique half: constructing proofs by chaining facts (not measuring), finding and explaining errors in a peer's working, and the signature move of disproving a false 'always' conjecture with a single counter-example. Learners meet the proof asymmetry — one honest counter-example kills a universal claim, while confirming examples cannot establish it unless every possible case is checked (impossible for claims about all numbers) — and the logic of implication, including the claim/converse distinction. Activities span fractions, ratio, algebra and geometry, with a live adversarial dialogue as the primary vehicle and a manipulable conjecture/proof workspace, static critique cards, and a recognition warm-up as complementary alternatives serving different purposes.

activities.title: The confident conjecture champion (adversarial dialogue)
feedback: Revoice and extend the learner's chain rather than scoring it; when they offer only confirming examples, press 'so is it proved, or could there still be a breaker?'
If they name a counter-example, ask them to say exactly why that one case is enough to sink the whole 'always' rule.

When they repair the champion's fraction-division flip, ask them to state which step was wrong and what the correct step is (inverting the divisor, not the first fraction), not just that the answer looked odd.
Separate convincing from justifying: if an explanation sounds confident but has gaps, name it as convincing; if it is a complete because/therefore chain, name it as justifying.
activities.rationale: Defending a proof against a skeptic and disproving a confident false claim are naturally real-time exchanges; a responsive adversary can press on the learner's specific gaps and adapt to a patched claim or a converse in a way a fixed artefact cannot — an affordance of responsiveness, not a claim that only dialogue can teach this logic (the workspace activity also makes the if/therefore structure tangible). This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures; use counterexamples; distinguish correct logic from flawed and explain the flaw; older students can compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments.

A general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false; empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the shift to understanding logical implication (and the claim/converse distinction) is slow and fragile, so one counter-example being decisive is a hard-won idea.

Primary proof types include proof by counter-example; specific confirming examples do not constitute a watertight proof, and recognising this is a key step on the describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder.
learnerActions: Face an in-role character who asserts a universal claim with total confidence: 'Multiplying ALWAYS makes a number bigger — I've tried 3×4, 5×6, 10×10, works every time. So it's proved, right?'
Decide whether piling up more agreeing examples settles it, or whether you must HUNT for a case that breaks the claim.
Produce and state a decisive counter-example, e.g. '6 times a half is three — that's smaller, so it's not always,' and explain why that single case is enough.

When the champion patches the claim ('okay, multiplying always makes bigger OR the same') test the patch again: × 1/2 still shrinks it (so it breaks the patch), while × 1 only reaches the 'same' boundary the patch now allows.

When the champion defends a flawed fraction division ('just flip the FIRST fraction') locate the faulty step, say why it fails, and give the correct method (invert the divisor — the second fraction — then multiply).

activities.title: Conjecture-testing and proof-building workspace
feedback: Report whether the chosen counter-example truly breaks the claim as scoped (for 'multiplying makes bigger': is the product actually not bigger, either smaller as with × 1/2 or equal as with × 1?), not merely whether a value was placed.

On the fraction-division panel, confirm whether the tapped step is the genuinely faulty one (inverting the first fraction instead of the divisor) and whether the selected method is correct.
activities.rationale: A manipulable workspace makes the decisive-single-case logic and the if/therefore structure tangible: dragging a value to watch a claim collapse and snapping facts into a chain externalise the reasoning. The live recolouring/collapse and drag interactions are illustrative mechanisms, not required tooling. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.

If including 'the more sides a shape has, the bigger its angles', state inside the task which angle is meant (e.g. each interior angle): for regular polygons each interior angle does grow with the number of sides, but it fails for irregular shapes, so it sorts as 'sometimes' — do not present it as a straightforwardly false 'always' claim.

Self-audit of worked examples: 6 × 1/2 = 3 is correct and is a valid counter-example to 'multiplying always makes bigger'; 8 × 0 = 0 is also valid. For the strict claim 'makes bigger', × 1 is also a breaker (6 × 1 = 6 is not bigger). The angle proof target of 60° is used illustratively and depends on the specific givens in a diagram — ensure the chained facts actually force 60° before presenting it to learners.

Comparative necessity over other media is NOT established by the sources provided; the original's 'only live dialogue teaches this' framing has been reduced to the narrow affordance of real-time responsiveness to the learner's gaps.

The patched claim 'multiplying always makes bigger OR the same' remains false for 0 < factor < 1 (× 1/2 shrinks), so × 1/2 is still a valid breaker; × 1 only reaches the 'same' boundary the patch allows and no longer breaks the patched claim. Keep the two tests distinct when guiding learners.

The flawed fraction-division cue 'flip/invert the first fraction' is a deliberate error to be critiqued (the divisor, i.e. the second fraction, is the one inverted); ensure it is always framed as the error to find, never as a method to follow.

The conjecture 'the more sides a shape has, the bigger its angles' is now scoped in-activity as a 'sometimes' claim: each interior angle of a regular polygon does grow with sides (triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°...), but it fails for irregular shapes and for exterior angles. The original pedagogy's treatment of it as flatly false is imprecise; specify the intended angle type before using it.

probeDeeper: 'How many examples where it works would it take to PROVE the rule always holds? And how many where it fails to prove it doesn't?'

errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a genuine false belief about multiplication — confront with scaling: 'what is 6 lots of a half?' Reteach multiplication as scaling (× less than 1 shrinks) using a picture, not just the argument skill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child agrees the rule is true, or tests only whole numbers and confirms it; when nudged, cannot see why a fraction would behave differently.

errorPatterns.pattern: Empirical proof scheme: responds to 'prove it's wrong' by trying MORE examples, or judges the rule 'usually/mostly true', not grasping that one counter-example is decisive and confirming cases never prove an 'always'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the asymmetry explicitly: 'How many YES examples would prove an ALWAYS? How many NO examples to disprove it?' Elicit that one counter-example is enough; celebrate finding the breaker over listing confirmers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child piles up examples on either side, or says 'it's right most of the time' — treats proof as accumulation of cases rather than a single decisive breaker.

errorPatterns.pattern: Suspects the rule is false and rejects the example-piling, but cannot yet find or articulate the counter-example — the deductive instinct is present but the productive step lags.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT read as not-knowing. Prompt the search without giving the answer: 'you think there's a case — what if one of the numbers were less than 1? Try a half.' Let the child produce and state the breaker; the logic of implication is already forming.

responseLevels.gap: Endorses the rule, or tries only whole numbers and confirms it, or says 'mostly true'; does not produce a counter-example.
responseLevels.full: Produces a factor-below-1 counter-example (6 × 1/2 = 3, or ×0) AND states that a single such case disproves the 'always' claim while no number of confirming cases could prove it — then applies the same counter-example strategy unprompted to a repaired or new conjecture (e.g. the converse or the '≥' patch).
responseLevels.partial: Suspects or states the rule is false, or even offers a fractional case, but cannot explain why one counter-example is DECISIVE — may still want more cases to be sure, or gets the verdict without the sufficiency reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate is sure of this rule: 'When you multiply two numbers, the answer is always bigger than both of them — I've tried loads and it always works.' Are they right? assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands proof-by-counter-example knows that a single case with a factor below 1 settles it decisively, and reaches for one; a child in the empirical scheme keeps testing whole numbers, confirms the rule, or says 'mostly true' — never grasping that one breaker overturns 'always'. The prompt is hard to answer right for the wrong reason: guessing 'wrong' isn't enough; the discriminating act is generating the decisive case AND stating that one is sufficient. pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, strategic tool use begins as CHOOSING among familiar concrete tools (cubes, counters, fingers, ten frame) and being able to say WHY that tool helps this problem. Name each tool's limitation in play — 'fingers run out past ten', 'a ten frame only holds ten' — so children begin weighing fit rather than habit
Keep tools as thinking aids and model solving a small, known fact WITHOUT a tool afterwards, so reliance does not set in (EEF: manipulatives are a temporary scaffold)
Value the explanation as much as the answer — a child who solved it but cannot say why the tool helped has not yet met this practice

The learning lives in the reason, not fluent handling. Offer a genuine choice rather than prescribing a tool, let a tool's limitation be felt in action (using fingers to show both parts of 8+7 runs past ten), and press for a fit-reason tied to the numbers. Keep tools as temporary scaffolds and model solving a small known fact without a tool so reliance does not set in.

activities.title: The tool tray: 8 + 7 and 3 + 2
feedback: If fingers are chosen for 8+7 and used to show both parts, let the count pass ten so the limitation is felt rather than told, then ask what else the tray offers.

After solving, ask why this tool and strategy helped. Accept a reason tied to the numbers or representation, including a valid counting-on explanation with fingers. If the child tried to show all15 objects simultaneously, discuss that specific ten-finger limitation and compare it with the ten frame.
If the ten frame is filled correctly but the reason is only 'because you're meant to', ask what the frame SHOWS: 'how many empty spaces to ten?'
For 3+2, confirm fingers fit well here, so the choice genuinely depends on the numbers.

Try the ten frame instead: place 8 (nearly filling one frame), then split the 7 — 2 completes the first ten, and the remaining 5 go beside the full frame (or into a second frame), giving 'fill to ten, then five more — fifteen.'

A child who insists on a tool for a fact they genuinely already know (e.g. 2+1) is likely showing reliance on the scaffold rather than a conceptual gap — gently invite them to try without the tool to build confidence, and only revisit counting if the fact turns out not to be secure.

pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, 'making sense of a problem' means the child learns that a word problem describes a real situation to be understood before any number is touched. The proficient young solver restates what the story is asking in their own words, represents it with objects or a drawing, works toward an answer, and then checks whether that answer makes sense in the story. The single biggest teaching risk is the opposite habit: children being conditioned to grab the numbers and 'do a sum', a compulsion to calculate that suspends real-world sense-making. activities.title: The thinking partner who won't take a number yet
feedback: When the child retells the story and names what is asked before computing, affirm that move explicitly: that understanding-first step is the goal.
If the child blurts a number, the partner does not accept it yet — it asks 'what is happening?' and 'how could you show that with your counters?'
When the child catches an unanswerable story ('that doesn't make sense, you can't work that out!'), the partner delights in the catch — this is the target moment.
Always close solvable stories with 'does your answer make sense in the story?' to plant the reasonableness habit.
activities.rationale: The topic is a dialogic habit: understanding the story and explaining a pathway before computing. A partner that poses a short story, asks self-questioning prompts, and refuses a bare number models the self-questioning routine; the occasional nonsensical story directly confronts the compulsion to calculate. Spoken or tapped responses keep turns short for this age. This is a proposed design, not a tested intervention.

Show the story with counters/frogs or fingers ('show me with your frogs') so the part-part-whole structure is visible.
Work out an answer for a solvable story, then answer the partner's closing question: 'Does your answer make sense in the story?'

activities.intendedInsight: A word problem is a situation to understand, not just numbers to do a sum with; sense-making and a reasonableness check come before and after calculating.

activities.title: Numberless, progressively-revealed story with a part-whole workspace

activities.rationale: Staging the reveal (picture, then question, then numbers) and giving a part-whole mat with draggable counters lets the child build a representation before a number invites computing, countering the compulsion to calculate and building the visual-representation skill. activities.title: Tap-to-reveal worked example of the four moves

activities.title: Single reasonableness check (which answer could not be right?)

assess.correctAnswer: There is no single scored answer — listen for a child who first makes sense of the situation: retells the story in their own words, names what is being asked (how many Maya has left), represents it (moves 6 counters and takes 2 away, or draws), gives 4, and can say why 4 makes sense (she started with 6 and lost some, so it must be fewer than 6). The disposition, not the arithmetic, is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compulsion to calculate with no real-world check: 'every problem is a sum you do with the numbers' — the child computes and stops, and will produce a number even for a story that can't be answered.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use numberless / progressively-revealed stories and occasional unanswerable ones; make 'does this make sense in real life?' a routine closing question. Confront the specific case: 'could we really know her age from the apples?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When told a nonsensical story ('5 red apples and 3 green apples — how old is the girl?'), the child confidently gives a number (usually 8) rather than saying it can't be worked out.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword operation-mapping: picks the operation from a cue word ('altogether' = add, 'gave away' = subtract) before reading or understanding the whole story.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Never use keyword posters; have the child retell the story and model it with objects so the structure, not the word, drives the choice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names an operation from one word and misfires when the word points the wrong way (e.g. a 'more' comparison story where the answer is found by subtracting).

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats being stuck as 'I can't do it' and abandons, rather than trying to represent the story another way.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach the concept: offer a representation ('let's put out the counters') and name the move — 'when it's tricky, we show it a different way'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child stops and says 'I don't get it' without attempting to act it out or draw; has the general persistence habit but doesn't yet apply it in maths.

responseLevels.gap: Jumps to a number without engaging the story; grabs the numbers and applies an operation; answers the nonsensical apples problem with a number and cannot say what is being asked.
responseLevels.full: Leads with the situation: retells the problem, represents it, and justifies the answer BY the story ('fewer than 6 because she gave some away'); spontaneously flags the unanswerable problem as making no sense, and transfers this to a new story unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Can restate the story and often gets the right number, but treats making-sense and checking as separate add-ons — recites 'understand, then check' or represents when prompted, yet does not spontaneously use the situation to justify or sense-check the answer.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Read the child a short within-10 story, e.g. 'Maya had 6 stickers. She gave 2 to her friend.' Then, before asking for any answer, ask: 'What is this story about — can you tell it back to me in your own words? What are we trying to find out? Show me how you'd work it out.' Finish with: 'How would you know if your answer makes sense?' Treat it as a discussion, not a test — you are surfacing how the child thinks about problems, not marking a number right or wrong.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who is genuinely making sense pauses on the STORY first — retells it, shows it, and can justify the answer by the situation ('fewer than 6 because she gave some away'). A child in the compulsion-to-calculate habit skips straight to a number and, tellingly, will still produce a number for a nonsensical story and cannot say why it makes sense. The gap shows in the reasoning and the sense-check, not in whether they can subtract.

pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, quantitative reasoning begins as a two-way translation between a real situation and a concrete or pictorial model: a child acts out 'five ducks and two more come' with cubes and connects the physical joining to the idea of addition, and can also go the other way — given a set of cubes, tell a matching story. The heart of the practice (CCSS MP2) is attending to the MEANING of the quantities, not just producing a total: knowing that THIS cube stands for a duck, that the 5 and the 2 are the parts and the whole group is the total, and that 'putting together' is what makes it addition. It is best taught through story-acting and the concrete→pictorial bridge the NCETM describes for the bar model's youngest form: line objects up, then stand a drawn bar beside them and ask 'what's the same, what's different?' so the picture is understood as an abstraction of the real thing rather than a decoration.
bestPractices: Act stories out with concrete objects first, then draw alongside, so the child sees the drawing as standing FOR the objects (NCETM's line-up→cubes→bar sequence with 'what's the same, what's different?')
Insist the child name the referent of each quantity ('the 5 is the ducks already there') — MP2's 'attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute'
Work translation in BOTH directions: situation→model AND model→story, so the child is not just illustrating answers but reading meaning off a representation
Pair children (one moves cubes, one draws/records) so the mapping between concrete and pictorial is talked aloud
Connect the physical action to the operation explicitly — putting together = addition, taking away = subtraction — rather than letting the child guess from words
keyRepresentations: Counters/cubes for acting out and combining/separating
Five-frame and ten-frame for structuring the quantities
Part-whole picture: two groups lined up with a drawn bar beside them (the bar model's earliest form)
Simple number sentence (with +, −) as the symbolic end of the concrete→pictorial→abstract bridge

Produces the total by counting all but cannot point to the parts or the action inside the model
Picks the operation from a word ('more' → add) rather than from what happens in the situation

learn.summary: For 5-6 year olds, quantitative reasoning is a two-way translation between a real situation and a concrete/pictorial model: acting out 'five ducks and two more swim up' with cubes, AND going the other way — given cubes, telling a matching story. The heart (CCSS MP2) is attending to the MEANING of quantities, not just producing a total: knowing THIS cube stands for a duck, that 5 and 2 are the parts and the whole is the total, and that 'putting together' is what makes it addition. Taught through story-acting and the concrete→pictorial bridge NCETM describes for the youngest bar model: line objects up, stand a drawn bar beside them, and ask 'what's the same, what's different?' so the picture is understood as an abstraction of the real thing.

activities.title: Build the story, then flip it
feedback: Name whether EACH number is mapped to the right part, not just whether the total is right (e.g. 'your 2 is sitting in the part for the ducks already there — which cubes are the ones that swam in?').
When the child flips it, respond to whether the invented story preserves the exact quantities and their referents, not just whether it sounds plausible.
If the child reaches 'seven' fast, prompt: 'show me where the 5 hides in your seven, and where the 2 is.'
activities.rationale: The practice IS translation between a situation and a model; a live builder where cubes, bar and number sentence assemble from the child's own action is intended to make the situation→symbol mapping felt rather than told, and the 'flip it' mode exercises the model→story direction so the child reads meaning off a representation rather than only illustrating answers. Highlighting each numeral over the cubes it refers to is intended to keep quantities attached to meaning (MP2). Dragging cubes, the bar snapping across and 'flip it' are optional concrete examples of the mechanism, not required implementation.
sourceClaims: MP2: mathematically proficient students attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; they create a coherent representation of the problem and can decontextualize (represent a situation symbolically) and contextualize (pause to probe the referents for the symbols).
learnerActions: Listen to or watch a short story: 'Five ducks bob on a pond, then two more paddle in.'
Drag/place five cubes into the left of a part-whole frame and two into the right to match the story.
Watch a bar form across the top and the sentence 5 + 2 = 7 appear, with the '5' marking the first cubes and the '2' marking the newcomers.
Point to which cubes are the 5, which are the 2, and show the whole group.

'Flip it': take a pile of cubes already split (e.g. 4 and 3) and invent a story the picture could tell — then notice the SAME cubes could be 'four birds and three more' OR 'seven birds, three flew off'.
activities.intendedInsight: The model carries meaning in both directions: numbers stand for ducks, the joining stands for adding, and the child can travel from world to symbol and back — the model is not a picture of an answer but a thing that holds a relationship.

activities.title: Line up, cubes, bar — what's the same, what's different?
feedback: If the child treats the model as two separate amounts, push the groups together under one drawn bar and re-ask 'what's the same, what's different?'.
Confirm when the child can name a part and the whole: 'yes — the 5 and the 2 are the parts, and all of them together is the whole group.'
activities.rationale: NCETM's concrete→pictorial sequence for the youngest learners (line up → linking cubes → drawn bar alongside, with 'what's the same, what's different?') bridges concrete experience and abstract symbols and is intended to address the misconception of reading the model as separate amounts rather than a relationship.
sourceClaims: For the youngest children the bar/part-whole representation should be built from concrete experience — line objects up, replace with linking cubes and a drawn bar alongside, and ask 'what's the same, what's different?' to help children make sense of the bar as an abstraction; it bridges concrete experience and abstract symbols and is introduced in Year 1.
learnerActions: Line real objects (toy ducks, counters) up to match a told situation.
Replace them with linking cubes, then stand a drawn bar alongside the cubes.
Compare: 'What's the same between the cubes and the bar? What's different?'
Push the two groups together under one bar to show the whole being made of parts.
activities.intendedInsight: The bar/picture is an abstraction OF the real objects, not a decoration — and the two parts combine into one whole (part-part-whole), not two unrelated piles.

activities.title: Talk it through with a story partner
feedback: Never scored. When a child's story drops the numbers, revoice: 'you said some ducks — exactly how many? show me on the cubes,' and let them re-tell with the numbers in.
Press gently on the action: 'what did the ducks DO in my story? show me that happening with your cubes.'
activities.rationale: Naming referents and telling a matching story is dialogic; an in-role partner can push the child to keep quantities and the action attached to meaning, and pairing (one moves cubes, one records) makes the concrete↔pictorial mapping talked aloud. This supports the model→story direction and MP2's probing of the referents for the symbols.
sourceClaims: MP2: mathematically proficient students attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; they create a coherent representation of the problem and can decontextualize (represent a situation symbolically) and contextualize (pause to probe the referents for the symbols).
learnerActions: Listen to a partner (an adult, peer, or in-role puppet) tell a story and build it with cubes.
Answer 'where's the 5 in your cubes? which bit is the 2? what happened to make it the whole group?'
When the partner builds a model, say what story it could be — keeping the exact numbers in.
In pairs, one child moves the cubes while the other draws/records, talking the mapping aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming what each quantity refers to, and the action that joins them, keeps the numbers attached to meaning; saying it aloud makes the concrete→pictorial mapping explicit.

activities.title: Worked example: the pond scene (scaffold)
feedback: Use as a shared talking point: 'the 5 is the ducks already on the pond — where's the 2?' Then move the child to building and flipping their own, where they do the translation.
activities.rationale: A fixed, reveal-based scene can show one worked situation→sentence mapping as a clear example before the child does the productive, two-way work. It illustrates a connection; it does not elicit the child's own construction or let them vary the quantities, so it belongs before the builder, not as the assessment.
learnerActions: Look at a fixed pond scene; reveal '5' over the ducks already there and '2' over the arrivals.
Open a flap to see the matching sentence 5 + 2 = 7.
Talk about which part of the picture each number stands for before moving to building your own.
activities.intendedInsight: In this described situation the joining action points to addition, shown here as 5 + 2 = 7 (other true sentences such as 2 + 5 = 7 or 7 = 5 + 2 describe the same relationship), and each number refers to a specific group in the scene; note that a static set of cubes, by contrast, could tell several stories (as in 'flip it').

constraints: The productive core is CONSTRUCTING the model and explaining what each part represents, and working the translation BOTH ways (situation→model and model→story). Recognition-only tasks (e.g. 'which number sentence matches this picture?') can at most serve as a brief warm-up; a correct match does not show the child can build the model or map the parts, so do not read a match score as evidence of quantitative reasoning.
A fixed reveal/tap scene is a worked example only: it cannot let the child do the two-way translation or vary the quantities. Use it before the builder, not as assessment.

Assessment should not stop at the total: both a reasoning child and a compute-only child may say 'seven'. Listen for the mapping (which cubes are the 5, which the 2) and the joining action, which are hard to fake without the meaning.

When a child tells a vague story that loses the exact numbers (e.g. 'some ducks and some more'), do not mark it wrong — the reasoning may be present while the language of quantity is still forming; scribe/revoice to recover the precise numbers.
Do not let the child pick the operation from a word ('more' → add); connect the operation to what actually happens in the situation (putting together = addition, taking away = subtraction).

The original row rated a 3D interactive as adding nothing ('not a spatial-3D concept; 2D cubes and bars convey it better'). This rewrite does not propagate that as a universal claim — for combining small quantities, flat cube/bar representations are well-suited, but this is a fit judgement, not a proof that 3D cannot teach it.

The original rated a scored match 'poor' and a static image 'possible' partly on catalog-fit grounds. Retained here as objective scope limits (recognition-only does not elicit construction; a fixed scene cannot be manipulated), not as 'a scored task only assesses' or 'a static image cannot teach' absolutes.

Interactive mechanisms (dragging cubes, bar snapping across, numerals highlighting the cubes they refer to, 'flip it' mode) are preserved as OPTIONAL concrete examples of the learning mechanism, not mandatory implementation.
Arithmetic checked: 5 + 2 = 7 and the flip example 4 + 3 = 7 are correct; 'seven birds, three flew off' leaves 4, consistent with the 4/3 split shown.

probeDeeper: 'Point to the exact cubes that are the 2. How do you know those are the 2 and not part of the 5?'
'What did the ducks DO in my story? Show me that happening with your cubes.'
'Now YOU tell me a different story that these same cubes could be about.'
'If I take the 2 newcomers away again, how many ducks are on the pond? Show me why.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child mapping each quantity to its referent (5 = ducks already there, 2 = ducks that came) AND showing the joining action that makes the whole group, so the cubes are read as a relationship (parts making a whole), not two separate piles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the model as two separate amounts, not a relationship: builds 5 and 2 but cannot identify the whole or show that joining them makes it — sees a picture, not a part-part-whole.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the part-whole physically: push the two groups together under one drawn bar and ask 'what's the same, what's different?'; reteach representing the situation with objects so the relationship, not just the amounts, is modelled.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child lays out or counts the cubes but, asked to show the whole group or the joining, either recounts from 1 or treats the two piles as unrelated; cannot say which is a part and which is the whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses the exact quantities when going model→story: given cubes, tells a vague story ('some ducks and some more') that doesn't preserve the 5 and the 2 or their referents.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark wrong. Scribe/revoice: 'you said some ducks — exactly how many? show me on the cubes.' Let the child re-tell with the numbers in; the reasoning is present, only the telling lags.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reverses the translation but the story drops the precise numbers or what they stand for; the child clearly has the idea but the language of quantity is still forming.

errorPatterns.pattern: Produces the total but not the structure: jumps to 'seven' and counts all, unable to point to the parts or the action inside the model.

pedagogy.summary: At 5-6 mathematical modelling is at its simplest: use objects, a drawing, or a dictated number sentence to REPRESENT a real situation, and then read an answer back off the model — 'I had 5 apples and ate 2' becomes five cubes with two removed, and the child says three are left (CCSS MP4: in early grades this is as simple as writing an equation to describe a situation). The seed of the domain's biggest hazard — 'suspension of sense-making', where children compute without checking the story (CDE) — can be headed off here by always asking 'does your model match what happened?' and 'three what?'. Teaching is concrete, story-driven, and two-way (situation→model and model→story).

The central hazard to head off is 'suspension of sense-making' — computing without checking the story — addressed by habitually asking 'does your model match what happened?' and 'three what?'. Teaching is concrete, story-driven, and two-way (situation→model and model→story).

activities.title: Act the story on cubes, then read the answer back
feedback: If the child models 5 and 2 more (joining) instead of removing, act the eating out with real objects so the taking-away is physical, then ask them to redo the model to show removal.

If the child gives only 'three' with no meaning, do not mark it wrong — interpreting-back is just emerging; model the full sentence 'three apples left' and invite them to repeat it. The habit grows with repetition.

If the child reaches an answer bigger than 5 (more apples after eating some) and is untroubled, ask 'Can you have MORE apples after eating some?' to build the habit of checking the answer against what happened.
Confirm success when the child removes two to model the eating, says 'three apples left', and notices if a model contradicts the story.
activities.rationale: Acting the story on objects and reading the answer back is the simplest form of modelling with mathematics; in early grades this is as simple as writing an equation to describe a situation and interpreting the result in context. A five-frame/ten-frame can help structure the quantities. An optional story-modeller (animated scene plays, child drags/removes cubes, the number sentence builds itself, a 'does it match?' replay compares the child's model to the story) may make the mechanism concrete, but counters and drawings do the same work.

Check the model against the story: 'Does what I did to the cubes match what happened to the apples?'

activities.title: Work both directions: invent a story from a model
feedback: If the child only names numbers without an action, prompt 'What happened to go from five to three?' so they supply the taking-away.

activities.rationale: Working story→objects and objects→story helps the child understand the model as standing for the situation rather than as decoration or bare digits. learnerActions: Receive a model, e.g. a bowl that started at five and now holds three cubes

activities.intendedInsight: A model carries the whole situation — action and all — both ways: a story can be turned into a model, and a model can be read back as a story.

activities.title: Puppet tells a story and sometimes gets it wrong

If the child accepts the puppet's impossible answer, ask 'Can you have more apples after eating some?' and revisit the action.

Build the model and say what the answer means ('three apples left')
Catch the puppet when it models the story wrongly, e.g. 'I had 5 apples and I ate 2, so now I have 7?' — explain why that can't be right
Tell the puppet your own story for a model it shows you
activities.intendedInsight: Telling a matching story and interpreting what the answer means is a two-way, sense-making conversation; an answer that contradicts the story (more apples after eating some) must be rejected.

activities.title: Diagnostic: does the friend's drawing match the story?
feedback: If the child says the friend's drawing is fine, act the eating out with real objects so the taking-away is physical, then reteach representing a subtraction story with objects/drawings that show the action (the prerequisite skill).
If the child models removal but says only 'three', model 'three apples left' and invite them to say it; do not mark this wrong, as interpreting-back is just emerging.

Full success: models the eating as removal, catches that the friend's drawing adds instead, reads the answer back as 'three apples left', and checks it makes sense. (Inventing a matching story from a model is not asked for in this diagnostic, so check it separately, e.g. with the 'work both directions' activity.)
activities.rationale: The mismatch between the story's taking-away action and the friend's joining drawing is the hinge — hard to catch without mapping the situation to the model, easy to miss if only the numbers are attended to. This may discriminate children who model from those who just process digits.

learnerActions: Hear the story: 'I had 5 apples and I ate 2 of them'
Look at a friend's drawing that shows 5 apples and then 2 MORE apples drawn next to them
Decide whether the friend's drawing matches the story, and explain why or why not

Say what your answer means about the apples ('three apples left')

constraints: Model the ACTION, not just the numbers: 'ate 2' must be shown as removal, and the model must be checked against what actually happened.

A static tap-to-reveal scene (tap apples to see '5', tap eaten ones to see '−2', flap reveals '3 left') can present one worked example mapping a situation to a number sentence, but it is a scaffold: it cannot let the child act out the situation, vary it, or build their own model.

A scored 'which sentence matches?' item tests recognition and does not by itself elicit the child building a model that preserves the action or interpreting the answer in the story; use at most as a brief warm-up, not as the main activity.

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7 the modelling cycle becomes explicit at both ends: represent a measurement or money problem with a number sentence, bar model, or diagram, AND interpret the numerical answer back in context ('15 cm means the ribbon is 15 centimetres long') (CCSS MP4). Bar models now carry two-step and comparison structures. The defining new demand — and the one teachers most often skip — is the return trip: a bare '5' is not an answer to 'how much is left?'; the answer is '5p change'. This is exactly where 'suspension of sense-making' (CDE) does its damage: children compute and stop, without asking whether the number is reasonable or what it means. The CDE guide warns that stripping problems down to numbers and keywords ('take away means subtract') actively reinforces the habit; the remedy is to reason about the situation first and always interpret and sense-check the result.

The defining new demand is that a bare number is not an answer; the remedy to 'suspension of sense-making' is to reason about the situation before computing and always interpret and sense-check the result afterwards.

activities.title: Model a shop story, then make the return trip
feedback: If the child stops at a bare '5': ask 'five what? what is that for Sam?' — the calculation is right, only the interpretation needs prompting.
If the child endorses 35: 'you gave 20p and want 35p back — can you get more money by spending some?' Let them catch and reject the impossibility, then state the real change as '5p change'.
Direct feedback at the interpretation and the sense-check, not only at whether the arithmetic was correct.
activities.rationale: Building and then being required to interpret and sense-check makes the situation-answer link explicit; an optional live reasonableness gate (a slider or thumbs that flags impossible answers such as change > amount paid) and a required 'what does it mean?' step make the return trip concrete rather than skippable.

Work out the missing part to land on 5.
Complete a mandatory 'what does your 5 mean?' step: attach the unit and quantity, finishing the sentence '5p change'.
Pass a reasonableness check before the answer is accepted: decide whether a candidate answer could possibly be true in the story (e.g. flag that change greater than the amount paid is impossible).

Ask 'what does this number mean here?' at the end, not just 'what's the answer?'

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, real-world maths modelling means running the full cycle — choose a representation that fits the situation's structure, build it, compute, then interpret the result back in the right units with a plausibility check. At this age the new skill is SELECTING among competing models (percentage bar, scale diagram, double number line/ratio table, area rectangle) rather than being handed one. The recurring failure is answering with a by-product of the calculation (the discount £10, or the proportion 0.75) rather than the quantity the situation actually asked for (the £30 a shopper pays), and never sense-checking (a sale price must be below the original).

activities.title: Choose, build, interpret back: a modelling workbench
feedback: If a learner names £10 as the price: draw the percentage bar and shade discount vs part-left — 'you found the bit taken OFF; the price is the bit that STAYS'. Ask 'what does the shopper actually hand over?'

If a learner leaves 0.75 or 75 as the answer: ask '0.75 of WHAT?' and require conversion to £30 stated as money — a percentage answer ends in the unit of the quantity it is a percentage of, which here is pounds

If a learner subtracts 25 ('25% off means take 25') to get £15: anchor the percentage to the bar of £40 — 25% is a quarter OF this strip = £10 — and contrast 25% of £40 (=£10) with 25% of £80 (=£20) to show it depends on the amount

If a learner reports the carpet answer in a length unit (cm or m) or adds the sides for an area question: keep area and length physically distinct — coverage of the floor is a squared unit (m² or cm²), the edge measured is a length (m or cm) — and do not proceed until the unit matches the quantity, with the squared area unit matching the length unit used (a room measured in metres gives m², so 4 m × 3 m = 12 m²)
activities.rationale: Modelling explicitly includes interpreting results in context and reflecting on whether they make sense; a part-whole/percentage bar exposes proportional structure so a child can find and explain a sale price rather than manipulating numbers by rule. Building the situation model before computing, and making representation choice explicit, targets the age-appropriate skill of selecting rather than just using a model.

Pass an interpret-back gate: state the final answer with its unit (£30) and check it is reasonable — a sale price must be less than £40

Re-run the same process on a room-carpet problem (choose a scale diagram, apply the area formula, and give the area in a squared unit that matches the length unit of the measurements — e.g. a 4 m × 3 m room needs 12 m² of carpet) and a recipe-scaling problem (choose a double number line, answer in grams)

activities.rationale: Articulating the interpret-back in words can help the learner attach each number to its referent and defend reasonableness — the discriminating skill, since both wrong answers are genuine by-products of a correct calculation. activities.title: Feel area as coverage, length as edge (optional spatial scaffold)
feedback: If a learner gives a length where an area is needed, or drops the squared unit, return to the physical distinction: coverage fills the floor (a squared unit), the edge runs around it (a length unit), and the squared unit must match the length unit used
activities.rationale: A room may make area-versus-perimeter felt for learners who confuse them, but the core structures at this age (percentage, rate, scale) are planar or numeric, so this remains subordinate to the 2D modelling work and should not displace it. Its benefit for most learners is untested; offer it where the area/length confusion is observed.
learnerActions: Cover the floor of a room to feel area as coverage, reported in a squared unit matching the measurements (e.g. m² of carpet needed for a metre-dimensioned room)

constraints: The modelling cycle is the objective: choosing a representation, computing, AND interpreting back with a reasonableness check. A scored step that accepts a bare correct number cannot force or observe the representation-choice and interpret-back, so use such checks only for isolated sub-skills (e.g. percentage of an amount) that feed the real modelling task.

A static labelled percentage bar or scale diagram can prime or remind what a representation shows, but on its own does not let the learner choose, compute, or interpret back; treat it as a reference card, not the teaching vehicle for the practice.

Keep area and length as distinct quantities with distinct units throughout; the area uses a squared unit (m² or cm²) that matches the length unit of the measurements and must not be reported as a length.

Every percentage answer must return to the real quantity the situation asks for, stated with its unit (e.g. the £30 a shopper actually pays when the question asks for the price paid) — never leave a bare 30, 75, or 0.75.
Enlarging a recipe or shape is multiplicative (scale by a factor), not additive (add the same amount); watch for additive scaling.
The room/coverage activity is an optional scaffold for learners who confuse area and perimeter, not a required step for every learner.

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 modelling reaches its primary-school capstone: ratio, scale, volume and proportional reasoning, and — decisively — deciding whether an answer should be rounded and to what accuracy. This is where the interpret-back becomes a judgement, not just a re-labelling: the classic case is the bus problem (328 people, 40-seat buses → 8.2 → you must order 9 whole buses), where the mathematically 'exact' answer is the wrong answer to the real question. The teaching goal is a child who chooses a fit-for-purpose tool (bar, double number line, ratio table, labelled diagram + formula), computes, and then asks 'what does this decimal mean here — do I round, which way, and to what precision?' before trusting it.

Use authentic 'order the buses / fill the boxes' framings where rounding the wrong way fails visibly — research shows far more children reason correctly when the context is real than when the division is bare (DeFranco & Curcio)
Teach tool CHOICE for proportional problems: double number line and ratio table for ratio/rate, labelled diagram + formula for volume, scale factor for similar shapes
Keep units alive through volume work (cm³ vs cm² vs cm) and interpret the final quantity as a real capacity a container could hold
Demand a reasonableness pass on every model: estimate first, then check the computed answer sits near the estimate and makes sense in the situation

learn.summary: For 10-11 year olds, this is the capstone of mathematical modelling: choosing a fit-for-purpose tool (bar model, double number line, ratio table, labelled 3D diagram + volume formula, scale factor), computing, and then making the decisive judgement — does this answer need rounding, which way, and to what accuracy, and does the SITUATION rather than a rote rule decide? The anchor case is the bus problem (328 people, 40-seat coaches → 8.2 → you must book 9), where the 'exact' decimal is the wrong real answer. Core activities put the child in authentic decisions where naive rounding visibly fails, kept alongside spatial volume work and a dialogue variant that presses for a committed, justified answer.

activities.title: Order the coaches: when 8.2 is the wrong answer
feedback: If a learner reports '8.2 coaches' untroubled, ask: 'Can the organiser book two-tenths of a coach? What can they actually order?' Route the quotient back to a bookable whole.

If a learner rounds down to 8 citing '.2 rounds down', ask them to work out 8 × 40 and compare with 328 — surface the 8 people with no seat, then establish that here the context forces rounding UP however small the remainder.
For the 320-people case, affirm that an exact quotient (8) needs no rounding judgement, so the child can see the decision is driven by the leftover, not by habit.
When a learner commits to 9 and justifies it by the stranded people, affirm that they have modelled, not just computed.
For the crates variant, if a learner rounds up by habit, ask what a partly-filled crate means for a FULL-crate count, so they see the direction flips with the situation.
activities.rationale: Research cited for this topic reports children reason correctly about rounding far more often when a bare division is reframed as an authentic ordering task, so staging a real decision with a visible consequence targets the modelling judgement rather than the easy arithmetic.

In DeFranco & Curcio's bus problem (328 people, 40-seat buses), few children rounded to whole buses when the division was bare, but most reasoned correctly when the task was framed as authentically ordering the buses — context restores sense-making and drives rounding
learnerActions: Take the real job: 328 people need to travel to a match; each coach seats 40. Build a ratio table or double number line, or divide, and land on 8.2.
Make the rounding decision explicitly: do I round? which way? to what accuracy? and WHY — state the reason before trusting the number.
Check the consequence of rounding down: 8 coaches × 40 = 320 seats, leaving 8 people with no seat. Commit to 9 coaches and justify it by those stranded people.
Explain in your own words why the SITUATION (a coach is indivisible, nobody can be left behind) decides the direction, not the nearest-whole rule.
Try the exact-division contrast: if only 320 people travelled, 320 ÷ 40 = 8 exactly, so no rounding decision arises — notice the dilemma only appears when the division leaves a remainder.

Try a variant that rounds the OTHER way: 'how many FULL crates can we pack from 328 apples, 40 to a crate?' — here you round down to 8 full crates (8 apples left over). Explain why the direction differs.
activities.intendedInsight: A computed decimal must be interpreted back against the real question; whether and which way to round is a judgement the context makes, not a rule applied on autopilot. The same arithmetic rounds up for coaches and down for full crates, and when the division is exact (320 ÷ 40 = 8) there is no rounding decision at all.

activities.title: Choosing the right tool for a proportional problem
feedback: If a learner adds a constant to both quantities on a scale variant, show two rows of a ratio table and ask what you multiply the first row by to reach the second — reassert the multiplicative relationship.
If a learner reaches for a single bar that can't show the rate, ask where the second quantity lives on their diagram, and rebuild with a double number line or ratio table.
Affirm tool choices the learner can justify by the structure of the situation rather than by habit.
activities.rationale: Guidance cited here holds that bar models and part-whole/comparison diagrams expose proportional structure so children set up and solve rather than manipulate numbers by rule, which motivates explicit, structure-matched tool choice.
sourceClaims: Bar models and part-whole/comparison diagrams expose ratio and proportional structure so children can set up and solve rather than manipulate numbers by rule
learnerActions: Before computing, pick a tool that matches the structure: double number line or ratio table for ratio/rate, bar model for part-whole ratio and comparison, scale factor for similar shapes.

Scale multiplicatively, not additively: check that if one quantity is multiplied by a factor, the other is multiplied by the same factor, rather than adding the same amount to both.
Explain why a single bar that shows only one quantity would hide the rate, and choose a tool that doesn't.

activities.title: Volume as capacity: pack it, compute it, then decide the accuracy
